observations.title: The reliability of the reported Cash in Bank - Local Currency, Current Account (CIB - LCCA) account amounting to P8.072 billion, cannot be ascertained due to the following:
observations.description:
a. Existence of outstanding reconciling items in the Bank Reconciliation Statement (BRS) totaling P155.799 million and P142.181 million for additions and deductions, respectively, which remain unadjusted in the books;

b. Existence of variance totaling P96.510 million between the Subsidiary Ledgers (SL) balance of the OCAT and cashbook balance of the City Treasurer’s Office (CTO); and P160.925 million between the SL and the confirmed balances from Authorized Government Depository Banks (AGDBs); and

c. Existence of bank accounts for expropriated properties that were opened and confirmed by the bank as savings accounts and were recorded as CIB - LCCA under the General Fund (GF) books totaling P145.025 million.

The above conditions resulted in the misstatement of affected accounts contrary to Paragraph 27 of International Public Sector Accounting Standard (IPSAS) I, Item 3.0 of COA Circular No. 96-011 and Section 20 of COA Circular No. 92-382 dated July 3, 1992.

1.1. Paragraph 27 of IPSAS 1 provides that the FS shall present fairly the financial position, financial performance and cash flows of an entity. Fair presentation requires the faithful representation of the effects of transactions, other events, and conditions in accordance with the definitions and recognition criteria for assets, liabilities, revenue and expenses set out in IPSASs. The application of IPSASs, with additional disclosures when necessary, is presumed to result in financial statements that achieve a fair presentation.

1.2. Item 3.0 of COA Circular No. 96-011 requires that the Local Accountants, within 10 days from receipt of the Bank Statements (BS), shall reconcile the same with the General Ledgers (GL) and prepare the BRS in five copies. The Accountant shall draw Journal Entry Voucher (JEV) to record all valid reconciling items that require adjustment and correction in the GL. The duplicate and quadruplicate copies of the BRS, including the paid checks, original copies of debit/credit memos, shall be submitted to the Auditor concerned for verification within 10 days from the end of each month.

1.3. Section 20 of COA Circular No. 92-382 provides that provinces, cities, and municipalities may open a combined savings and current account or COMBO account for the GF and SEF in the duly authorized depository bank. The opening of the bank accounts shall be documented with a depository contract or other appropriate documentation required by the bank, signed by the local treasurer concerned on behalf of the local government unit. Deposits to the COMBO account shall be made only through the savings account, and withdrawals shall be made only by issuing checks to be drawn on approved vouchers against the current account.

1.5. Analysis of the CIB-LCCA balances reported by OCAT, AGDB’s confirmed balances, and cashbook balances submitted by the CTO disclosed the following:

Existence of outstanding reconciling items in the BRS

1.6. The submitted BRS on the CIB-LCCA shows that there were current and prior years’ (PY) book reconciling items in the net amount of P13,618,132.22, which were not adjusted in the SLs by the OCAT, as presented below:

1.7. Upon inquiry, the OCAT revealed that the accumulation of these reconciling items was due to the delayed submission of documents by the CTO to the OCAT for recording.

1.8. These reconciling items pertain to deposits/disbursements or credit/debit memos in the bank not yet recorded by OCAT due to the delay in the receipt of documents from CTO, checks not yet presented to the bank for payment within six months, clerical errors made by the OCAT in recording, and unrecorded disbursements by the OCAT.

Existence of unadjusted variance reported in the SL of OCAT and cashbook balance of the CTO; and between the OCAT’s SL and the AGDB’s confirmed balances.

1.9. The total CIB-LCCA as reflected in the OCAT’s records amounted to P8,071,734,233.38, while the CTO’s cashbook balance showed a total of P7,897,838,880.22, resulting in a discrepancy of P173,895,353.16, as summarized below:

1.12. The discrepancies between the OCAT and AGDB records were due to several unadjusted reconciling items in the books and/or reflected in the bank as of year-end.

Existence of bank accounts for expropriated properties that were opened and confirmed by the bank as savings accounts and were recorded as CIB-LCCA under the GF books totaling P145,025,084.72

1.14. As of December 31, 2024, there were 48 bank accounts opened for expropriated/expropriation of properties maintained by the City. These accounts were recorded as part of CIB-LCCA under the GF. However, upon inquiry and confirmation by the banks, these accounts were opened as savings accounts.

1.15. It should be noted that expropriation accounts fall under TF as defined under Section 2(b) of COA Circular 92-382 as [T]rust Funds which shall consist of private and public monies which have officially come into the possession of the local government or of a local government official or trustee, agent or administrator, or which have been received as a guaranty for the fulfillment of some obligation. A trust fund shall only be used for the specific purpose for which it was created or for which it came into the possession of the local government unit.

1.16. The cited variances between balances from OCAT, CTO, and depository banks; and incomplete submission of BRS, non-adjustment of reconciling items, inclusion of various voided checks and misclassification of bank accounts resulted in the unreliability of the CIB as of December 31, 2024.

observations.title: There were deficiencies in the grant and liquidation of cash advances, contrary to COA regulations to wit:
observations.description:
a. Cash advances amounting to P355.158 million remained unliquidated as of December 31, 2024, due to the non-submission of liquidation reports by Accountable Officers (AOs), contrary to Section 89 of PD No. 1445 and Sections 5.1.1, 5.1.3, 5.7 and 5.8 of COA Circular No. 97-002;

b. Cash Advances required for immediate liquidation and settlement totaling P106.136 million pertained to accounts of AOs who are already deceased, resigned, retired or separated from the City that have been aged two months to 19 years, contrary to Section 4.1.3 of COA Circular No. 97-002 dated February 10, 1997; and

c. Additional cash advances were granted to six AOs despite non-liquidation or non-settlement of their previous cash advances, which is contrary to Item 4.1.2 of COA Circular No. 97-002, resulting in difficulty of liquidation, improper/ unmonitored utilization and accumulation of cash advances.

These circumstances resulted in the accumulation of cash advances by AOs, which overstated the Receivable accounts and understated the related Expense accounts as of December 31, 2024.

2.1. Section 89 of PD No. 1445, otherwise known as the State Audit Code of the Philippines, provides that cash advances shall be reported on and liquidated as soon as the purpose for which it was given has been served. No additional cash advance shall be allowed to any official or employee unless the previous cash advance given to him is first settled or a proper accounting thereof is made.

2.2. Likewise, Sections 4.1.2 and 4.13 of COA Circular No. 97-002, dated February 10, 1997, state that no additional cash advances shall be allowed to any official or employee unless the previous cash advance given to him is first settled or a proper accounting thereof is made. A cash advance shall be reported on as soon as the purpose for which it was given has been served.

2.3. The following provisions of the same COA Circular provide the cash advance liquidation timelines of an AO, as follows:

5.1.1 Salaries, Wages, etc. - within five (5) days after each fifteen (15) day/end of the month pay period.

5.1.3 Official Travel - within sixty (60) days after return to the Philippines in the case of foreign travel or within thirty (30) days after return to his permanent official station in the case of local travel, as provided for in EO 248 and COA Circular No. 96-004

Failure of the AO to liquidate his cash advance within the prescribed period shall constitute a valid cause for the withholding of his salary and the instruction of other sanctions as provided for under paragraphs 9.2 and 9.3 hereof.

5.7 When a cash advance is no longer needed or has not been used for a period of two (2) months, it must be returned to or refunded immediately to the collecting officer.

5.8 All cash advances shall be fully liquidated at the end of each year. Except for petty cash fund, the AO shall refund any unexpended balance to the Cashier/Collecting Officer who will issue the necessary official receipt.

Cash Advances pertaining to the accounts of deceased, resigned, retired or already separated from the City

2.13. As provided in the provisions of COA Circular No. 2012-004, the demand for the immediate liquidation and settlement of outstanding cash advances also applies to the accounts of those already retired, separated from the service and transferred to another agency.

2.14. An inquiry with the OCAT officers disclosed that a request for relief of accountability was already forwarded to the COA for the account of the deceased AO. Also, they stated that these CAs were granted between CYs 2005 and 2018, during which they were not yet connected with the City.

Additional cash advances were granted to four AOs despite non-liquidation or non-settlement of their previous cash advances

2.15. From CYs 2022 to 2024, additional cash advances were granted to four AOs who had outstanding advances which remained unsettled until December 31, 2024, contrary to Item 4.1.2 of COA Circular No. 97-002, details as follows:

2.16. An inquiry with some AOs who have multiple CAs revealed that they are having difficulty collating supporting documents for the liquidation of their cash advances. The liquidation of clothing allowances took some time due to delays experienced by some recipients, including those related to uniform repairs and returns. Also, the AOs in-charge of the payment of salaries and employees of those still under payroll claimed that a cash advance covers only one or a cluster of departments; hence, there is a need to draw different cash advances simultaneously.

2.17. As stated in Section 5.1.3 of COA Circular No. 97-002, the salary of the erring AO may be withheld for failure to liquidate his or her cash advances within the period prescribed. Further, all cash advances must be fully liquidated at the end of the year pursuant to Section 5.8 of the same Circular.

2.18. Thus, the inability of accountable officers to submit liquidation documents for the outstanding cash advances is not in compliance with Section 89 of PD No. 1445 and COA Circular No. 97-002. Additionally, the practice of granting overlapping cash advances may lead to challenges in liquidation, improper or unmonitored utilization, and the accumulation of cash advances.

observations.title: The accuracy, existence and completeness of various receivables accounts as of December 31, 2024, cannot be ascertained due to the following:
observations.description:
a. Receivables totaling P276.143 million were recorded in total amount without SL details or supporting documentation to substantiate the composition of the balances;

b. Unsupported balances of Inter-Agency Receivables amounting to P23.682 million;

c. Misclassified tax credits amounting to P510.615 million in the Other Receivables - Others account and unrecorded Other Receivables amounting to P770.569 million; and

d. Unreconciled balance of P9.309 million due to non-recording of cleared dishonored checks under the Other Receivables - Dishonored Checks account.

These are contrary to Paragraph 27 of the IPSAS 1; Sections 111 and 112 of PD No. 1445; and Items 6.1 and 6.2 of COA Circular No. 2016-005, dated December 19, 2016.

3.1. Paragraph 27 of IPSAS 1 states that financial statements shall present fairly the financial position, financial performance, and cash flows of an entity. Fair presentation requires the faithful representation of the effects of transactions, other events, and conditions in accordance with the definitions and recognition criteria for assets, liabilities, revenue and expenses set out in IPSASs.

3.2. Section 111 – Keeping of accounts under PD No. 1445, known as the “State Audit Code of the Philippines”, provides that:

(1) The accounts of an agency shall be kept in such detail as is necessary to meet the agency's needs and, at the same time, be adequate to furnish the information needed by fiscal or control agencies of the government.

(2) The highest standards of honesty, objectivity, and consistency shall be observed in the keeping of accounts to safeguard against inaccurate or misleading information.

3.3. Section 112 – Recording of financial transactions under the same code provides that,

Each government agency shall record its financial transactions and operations conformably with generally accepted accounting principles and in accordance with pertinent laws and regulations.

3.4. Items 6.1 and 6.2 of COA Circular No. 2016-005 dated December 19, 2016, state that:

6.1 All government entities shall conduct regular monitoring and analysis of receivable accounts to ensure that those are collected when these become due and demandable and that cash advances and fund transfers are liquidated within the prescribed period depending upon their nature and purpose; and

6.2 All government entities shall prepare the schedule of all receivables, unliquidated cash advances, and fund transfers as of December 31, 2015, and quarterly thereafter.

| Due from National Government Agencies | 502,493,231.27 | P2,951,043.86 | P6,605,657.12 | 512,049,932.25 |

| Other Receivables | P1,299,057,201.76 | P187,921.73 | P6,281,743.71 | P1,305,526,867.20 |

3.6. Among these amounts, the Loans Receivable and Operating Lease Receivable accounts, amounting to P200,178,534.59 and P76,143,354.78, respectively, were recorded in bulk without the proper SLs.

3.7. Verification and analysis of the accounts revealed the following:

Receivables were recorded in total amount without any SL details or supporting documentation

3.8. The balances of the Loans Receivable - Others account amounting to P200,178,534.59, and Operating Lease Receivable account amounting to P76,143,354.78, are unreliable due to the existence of significant receivables that lack proper SLs, the absence of recorded/detailed composition, Aging Schedule for Receivable, and the inability to update records reflecting payments, contrary to Section 111 of PD No. 1445 and Items 6.1 and 6.2 of COA Circular No. 2016-005.

3.9. A review of the prior year’s Notes to Financial Statements disclosed that the Loans Receivable account amounting to P199,681,970.59 represents receivables from beneficiaries of the City’s "Land for the Landless" program. This account has remained non-moving for several years, without entries to record payments made by beneficiaries.

3.10. Our inquiry with the Manila Urban Settlements Office (MUSO), revealed that they have not submitted an updated list of beneficiaries, along with corresponding schedules of receivables and collections, to the OCAT. As a result, the OCAT was unable to accurately record collections or update account balances.

3.11. Moreover, the Operating Lease Receivable account, amounting to P76,143,354.78, pertains to uncollected rent from various lessees of the City’s properties. Records indicate that most of the amount was recorded as a result of previous audit recommendations. The last posting to the account was made in CY 2021, and since then, no subsequent updates or adjustments have been recorded to reflect rental payments made by lessees.

3.12. An inquiry with the Patrimonial Unit of the City General Services Office (CGSO), which manages leases, revealed that they regularly submit monthly reports to OCAT, providing updated information on receivables from rental properties.

3.13. Furthermore, a review of OCAT records showed that these receivable accounts are recorded as total amounts. This method of recording lacked the necessary breakdown of individual SLs for each lessee and beneficiary, that would normally provide details of specific receivables.

3.14. The absence of these individual ledgers or schedules significantly limits the ability to trace and validate the underlying transactions, verify the correctness of balances, and assess the accuracy of collections or payments associated with each account.

Unsupported and unconfirmed balances of Inter-Agency Receivables

3.15. There were six identified unsupported and unconfirmed Inter-Agency Receivables totaling P23,682,204.19. Confirmation Letters were sent to these National Government Agencies (NGAs) and Government Owned and Controlled Corporations (GOCCs) to verify the accuracy of the recorded balances in their books, and the reply letters revealed that these NGAs and GOCCs have no outstanding payable to the City, as follows:

| Name of Implementing/ Recipient Agency (per SL) | Per Books | Per Confirmation Letter | Difference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Due from NGAs - Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) | P6,326,752.36 | - | P6,326,752.36 |
| Due from NGAs - Department of Education (DEPED) | 5,034,271.00 | - | 5,034,271.00 |
| Due from NGAs - Philippine Statistics Authority | 1,864,656.50 | - | 1,864,656.50 |
| Due from NGAs - Bureau of Treasury | 3,991,326.58 | - | 3,991,326.58 |
| Due from GOCC - Metropolitan Water District (MWSS) | 5,234,258.15 | - | 5,234,258.15 |
| Due from GOCC - Central Bank of the Philippines | 1,230,939.60 | - | 1,230,939.60 |
| Total | P23,682,204.19 | - | P23,682,204.19 |

3.16. Inquiries with various City Offices, including the CGSO, CTO, and OCAT, and requests for documentation to support the balances of these Inter-Agency Receivables revealed that these Offices do not maintain any records or documentation on these receivables.

Misclassified tax credits in the Other Receivables - Others account and unrecorded Other Receivables

3.17. Records from OCAT under the Other Receivables account, classified as Other Receivables–Others, show an outstanding amount of P1,281,008,485.11. Bulk of this amount pertains to the sale of the Investment in a Joint Venture totaling P5,137,128,000.00.

3.18. During the audit, we identified a series of collections related to the sale, computed as follows:

| Date | Official Receipt (OR) No. | Amount | Remarks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1/17/2016 | 4898451 | P250,000,000.00 |  |
| 1/23/2018 | 6947285 | 250,000,000.00 |  |
| 4/8/2020 | 9446093 | 500,000,000.00 |  |
| 9/30/2020 | 9644447 | 1,227,125,668.00 |  |
| 1/6/2021 | 9803625 | 1,041,138,400.00 |  |
| 5/31/2021 | 10141760 | 770,569,200.00 | Recorded as Other Deferred Credits – ‘Corporation A’ Advance Payment should be Other Receivables |
| 12/23/2022 | No OR details were provided | 587,679,318.00 |  |
| 7/14/2022 | 0527145 / 0527146 | 510,615,414.00 | Should be a Tax Credit |
| Total Collections |  | 5,137,128,000.00 |  |
| Sales Price |  | P5,137,128,000.00 |  |

3.19. The amount of P770,569,200.00, with OR No. 10141760, was recorded in the books under Other Deferred Credits – ‘Corporation A’ Advance Payment instead of Other Receivables – Others. This overstates the Receivables account and the said Liability account. Additionally, verification with the CTO indicates that the amount of P510,615,414.00 pertains to the tax withheld related to the sale, which should not be included in the Other Receivables account.

Dormant balance due to the inability to record cleared dishonored checks under the Other Receivables – Dishonored Checks account.

3.20. As of December 31, 2024, the Other Receivables – Dishonored Checks account still reflects an outstanding balance of P9,308,634.34, arising from previous collections made by checks that were later dishonored. This balance includes P9,275,175.00 in the GF and P33,459.04 in the TF.

3.21. An inquiry with the CTO revealed that there are no outstanding dishonored checks in their records. Additionally, review of the CTO’s logbook shows that these dishonored checks were either replaced by the client and deposited or settled in cash within the same year they were presented for payment.

3.22. Per OCAT inquiry, the said amount was already long outstanding in their books and, details of which can no longer be traced or provided. The JEVs that were previously prepared to record the redeposit or settlement of these dishonored checks are either charged to the Real Property Tax (RPT) or Business Income account instead of reverting to the Other Receivable – Dishonored account. These resulted in the overstatement of the Accounts Receivable account.

3.23. Thus, the accuracy, existence, and completeness of the Loans Receivable - Others account, amounting to P200,178,534.59, and the Operating Lease Receivable account, amounting to P76,143,354.78 cannot be ascertained. Likewise, the following accounts are either over or understated:

observations.title: The balance of the RPT and Special Education Tax (SET) Receivable amounting to P15.773 billion and P10.885 billion, respectively, as of December 31, 2024, cannot be ascertained due to the following:
observations.description:
a. The RPT and SET Receivables per books do not tally with the total RPT Delinquencies recorded in the Real Property Tax Owners Delinquency Listing (RPTODL) by P1.207 billion, due to non-coordination between the OCAT and CTO, which resulted in unreconciled data, contrary to Paragraph 27 of IPSAS 1; and

b. No reasonable Allowance for Impairment was provided for RPT and SET Receivables despite the presence of balances that have remained outstanding for more than 10 years totaling P10.889 billion and P5.754 billion for RPT and SET, respectively, which is not in accordance with Paragraph 37 of IPSAS 3 to attain fair presentation as provided by IPSAS 1.

These have casted doubt on the accuracy, validity and reliability of the RPT and SET Receivable account balances.

4.1. Paragraph 27 of IPSAS 1 – Presentation of Financial Statements provides:

Financial statements shall present fairly the financial position, financial performance, and cash flows of an entity. Fair presentation requires the faithful representation of the effects of transactions, other events, and conditions in accordance with the definitions and recognition criteria for assets, liabilities, revenue, and expenses set out in IPSASs.

4.2. Likewise, Paragraph 37 of IPSAS 3 - Accounting Policies, Changes in Accounting Estimates and Errors states:

As a result of the uncertainties inherent in delivering services, conducting trading, or other activities, many items in financial statements cannot be measured with precision but can only be estimated. Estimation involves judgments based on the latest available, reliable information. For example, estimates may be required of:

a) Tax revenue due to government;

b) Bad debts arising from uncollected taxes; xxx

4.3. Further, Paragraph 67 of IPSAS 29 provides that an entity shall assess at the end of each reporting period whether there is any objective evidence that a financial asset or group of financial assets is impaired.

4.4. Moreover, Annex B of COA Circular 2015-009 or the Revised Chart of Accounts defines Allowance for Impairment – RPT/SET Receivable as the amount credited when there is objective evidence that the RPT Receivable is impaired and debited for collection of receivables, transfer or reversal of impairment.

4.5. The account balances and aging of RPT and SET Receivables, as of December 31, 2024, are presented below:

| Year | RPT Receivables | SET Receivables |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2024 | P1,343,313,812.82 | P3,262,933,538.15 |
| 2023 | 3,041,168,738.24 | 1,680,828,373.86 |
| 2022 | 4,364,010,014.78 | 2,426,033,023.28 |
| 2021 | 1,634,164,548.11 | 910,179,875.31 |
| 2020 and prior years | 5,389,897,069.38 | 2,604,688,706.84 |
| Total | P15,772,554,183.33 | P10,884,663,517.44 |

4.6. Relevant audit procedures and review of relevant documents/schedules provided by the City revealed the following:

Discrepancy between RPT and SET Receivables vis-à-vis Delinquency list

4.7. As of December 31, 2024, the ending balances of the RPT and SET Receivables accounts amounted to P15,772,554,183.33 and P10,884,663,517.44, respectively, or a total of P26,657,217,700.77.

4.8. For monitoring and control purposes, the CTO maintains the RPT Roll Registry (RPTRR), which contains the names of the taxpayers and the taxes due and collectible from them for the taxable year. Furthermore, the CTO also maintains the RPTODL, which contains the names of delinquent taxpayers along with their cumulative unpaid taxes for the current taxable year and any prior years.

4.9. On the other hand, the OCAT’s basis for the set-up of RPT and SET Receivables is based on the actual collections as indicated in the Real Property Tax Administration System (RPTAS)

4.10. Review and verification of RPTODL balances as of December 31, 2024, showed a total balance of P27,864,455,376.83, as summarized in the succeeding table:

| District | Number of Real Property Units (RPUs) | RPT Basic Tax | SEF Tax | Total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I | 17,495 | P4,046,800,931.57 | P2,057,882,271.46 | P6,104,683,203.03 |
| II | 11,681 | 1,235,067,813.01 | 655,753,630.20 | 1,890,821,443.21 |
| III | 9,195 | 1,843,024,231.98 | 1,003,020,958.30 | 2,846,045,190.28 |
| IV | 11,483 | 901,819,418.02 | 504,593,875.11 | 1,406,413,293.13 |
| V | 24,029 | 3,766,325,116.09 | 1,994,379,223.75 | 5,760,704,339.84 |
| VI | 18,544 | 6,514,417,927.68 | 3,341,369,979.66 | 9,855,787,907.34 |
| Total | 92,427 | P18,307,455,438.35 | P9,556,999,938.48 | P27,864,455,376.83 |

4.11. Comparison between the amounts presented in the FS and RPTODL as of December 31, 2024, showed a discrepancy of P1,207,237,676.06, as follows:

| Particular | Balance per FS | Balance per RPTODL | Discrepancy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RPT Receivables | P15,772,554,183.33 | P18,307,455,438.35 | (P2,534,901,255.02) |
| SET Receivables | 10,884,663,517.44 | 9,556,999,938.48 | 1,327,663,578.96 |
| Total | P26,657,217,700.77 | P27,864,455,376.83 | (P1,207,237,676.06) |

4.12. Inquiry with the OCAT revealed that the CTO was not able to provide them the RPTODL as of December 31, 2024. The different bases of setting up the RPT and SET by both offices also contributed to the discrepancy noted.

4.13. Furthermore, the OCAT does not maintain the GLs and SLs for RPT and SET Receivable accounts based on the RPTRR and Report of Collections from the CTO. This resulted in the discrepancy between the amount of RPT and SET receivables recorded in the books and the RPTODL maintained by the CTO, contrary to Paragraph 27 of IPSAS 1.

A reasonable Allowance for Impairment for RPT and SET Receivables was not provided despite the presence of RPT and SET receivables in the delinquency list that have been outstanding for more than 10 years

4.14. Review of the RPTODL revealed the following aging of RPT and SET receivables as of December 31, 2024:

| Aging Summary Per Delinquency Listing | Number of RPUs | RPT | SET |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Delinquent for more than 10 years | 53,303 | P10,889,112,622.22 | P5,754,227,413.22 |
| Delinquent for 1 to 10 years | 29,837 | 7,320,909,734.57 | 3,747,942,075.89 |
| Current Delinquency | 9,287 | 97,433,081.56 | 54,830,449.37 |
| Total | 92,427.00 | P18,307,455,438.35 | P9,556,999,938.48 |

4.15. It can be gleaned from the table above that RPT and SET Receivables amounting to P10,889,112,622.22 and P5,754,227,413.22 have been past due for more than 10 years.

4.16. These accumulated balances have no assurance of collectability. Paragraph 37 of IPSAS 3 allows estimation that involves judgments based on latest available information, particularly in forecasting bad debts/uncollectible taxes.

4.17. Moreover, the use of reasonable and reliable estimates is an essential part of preparing the FS in accordance with the fair presentation requirements under IPSAS 1.

4.18. The City, through the OCAT, could have established a reasonable accounting estimate on the Allowance for Impairment of RPT and SET Receivables to disclose a more accurate collectible balance to be presented in the FS.

observations.title: The tax collection strategies and remedies for RPT and SET delinquencies provided under pertinent Sections of RA No. 7160 were not optimally utilized by the City, as manifested by the following circumstances:
observations.description:
a. 12,680 Notices of Delinquencies were not received by or served to registered owners of RPUs due to non-updating of addresses and other pertinent information in the RPT Assessment Roll (RPTAR) and Tax Declarations (TDs);

b. Submission of a certified list of RPT delinquencies to the City Council and posting of Notice of Delinquencies (NOD) were not undertaken by the CTO within City Hall premises and in strategic locations in barangays where the delinquent RPUs are situated; and

c. Discrepancies noted between the TDs vis-à-vis the actual status of properties based on the Geographical Information System (GIS) of the CTO.

These conditions contributed to the accumulation of tax delinquencies totaling P27.864 billion, exclusive of interest, as of December 31, 2024, thus, depriving the City of essential income for the implementation of priority PPAs for the benefit of its constituents.

5.1. The applicable provisions of RA No. 7160 are set forth below:

Section 209. Duty of Registrar of Deeds to Appraise Assessor of Real Property Listed in Registry. -

(a) To ascertain whether or not any real property entered in the Registry of Property has escaped discovery and listing for the purpose of taxation, the Registrar of Deeds shall prepare and submit to the provincial, city or municipal assessor, within six (6) months from the date of effectivity of this Code and every year thereafter, an abstract of his registry, which shall include brief but sufficient description of the real properties entered therein, their present owners, and the dates of their most recent transfer or alienation accompanied by copies of corresponding deeds of sale, donation, or partition or other forms of alienation.

Section 254. Notice of Delinquency in the Payment of the Real Property Tax.

(a) When the real property tax or any other tax imposed under this Title becomes delinquent, the provincial, city or municipal treasurer shall immediately cause a notice of the delinquency to be posted at the main entrance of the provincial capitol, or city or municipal hall and in a publicly accessible and conspicuous place in each Barangay of the local government unit concerned. The notice of delinquency shall also be published once a week for two (2) consecutive weeks, in a newspaper of general circulation in the province, city, or municipality.

(b) Such notice shall specify the date upon which the tax became delinquent and shall state that personal property may be distrained to effect payment. It shall likewise state that at any time before the distraint of personal property, payment of the tax with surcharges, interests and penalties may be made in accordance with the next following Section, and unless the tax, surcharges and penalties are paid before the expiration of the year for which the tax is due except when the notice of assessment or special levy is contested administratively or judicially pursuant to the provisions of Chapter 3, Title II, Book II of this Code, the delinquent real property will be sold at public auction, and the title to the property will be vested in the purchaser, subject, however, to the right of the delinquent owner of the property or any person having legal interest therein to redeem the property within one (1) year from the date of sale.

Section 256. Remedies for the Collection of Real Property Tax.

For the collection of the basic real property tax and any other tax levied under this Title, the local government unit concerned may avail of the remedies by administrative action thru levy on real property or by judicial action.

Section 269. Treasurer to Certify Delinquencies Remaining Uncollected.

The provincial, city or municipal treasurer or their deputies shall prepare a certified list of all real property tax delinquencies which remained uncollected or unpaid for at least one (1) year in his jurisdiction, and a statement of the reason or reasons for such non-collection or nonpayment, and shall submit the same to the Sanggunian concerned on or before December thirty-first (31st) of the year immediately succeeding the year in which the delinquencies were incurred, with a request for assistance in the enforcement of the remedies for collection provided herein.

5.2. Furthermore, Sections 472 (b) (6 to 8) of RA No. 7160 provides the powers, among others, of the City Assessor:

(6) Prepare, install and maintain a system of tax mapping, showing graphically all property subject to assessment and gather all data concerning the same;

(7) Conduct frequent physical surveys to verify and determine whether all real property within the province are properly listed in the assessment rolls;

(8) Exercise the functions of appraisal and assessment primarily for taxation purposes of all real properties in the local government unit concerned; xxx

5.3. As of December 31, 2024, the RPTODL from the CTO show delinquencies for RPT and SET amounting to P27,864,455,376.83, as summarized below:

| District | Number of RPUs | RPT Basic Tax | SEF Tax | Total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I | 17,495 | P4,046,800,931.57 | P2,057,882,271.46 | P6,104,683,203.03 |
| II | 11,681 | 1,235,067,813.01 | 655,753,630.20 | 1,890,821,443.21 |
| III | 9,195 | 1,843,024,231.98 | 1,003,020,958.30 | 2,846,045,190.28 |
| IV | 11,483 | 901,819,418.02 | 504,593,875.11 | 1,406,413,293.13 |
| V | 24,029 | 3,766,325,116.09 | 1,994,379,223.75 | 5,760,704,339.84 |
| VI | 18,544 | 6,514,417,927.68 | 3,341,369,979.66 | 9,855,787,907.34 |
| Total | 92,427 | P18,307,455,438.35 | P9,556,999,938.48 | P27,864,455,376.83 |

5.4. Our audit disclosed the following:

12,680 out of 17,159 Notices of Delinquencies were not received by or served to registered owners of properties

5.5. A total of 17,159 Notices of Delinquency were issued in CY 2024. Details in the succeeding table.

First Notices of Delinquency processed as of December 31, 2024

| District | Registered Mail | Hand Carried | Total | Received/ Served | Not Received/ Served |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 514 | 74 | 588 | 441 | 147 |
| 2 | 35 | 26 | 61 | 33 | 28 |
| 3 | 2,380 | 322 | 2,702 | 814 | 1,888 |
| 4 | 4,078 | 211 | 4,289 | 426 | 3,863 |
| 5 | 7,560 | 224 | 7,784 | 1,829 | 5,955 |
| Subtotal | 14,567 | 857 | 15,424 | 3,543 | 11,881 |

Second Notices of Delinquency processed as of December 31, 2024

| District | Registered Mail | Hand Carried | Total | Received/ Served | Not Received/ Served |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 351 | 0 | 351 | 317 | 34 |
| 2 | 31 | 0 | 31 | 16 | 15 |
| 3 | 694 | 0 | 694 | 267 | 427 |
| 4 | 40 | 0 | 40 | 0 | 40 |
| 5 | 352 | 267 | 619 | 336 | 283 |
| Subtotal | 1,468 | 267 | 1,735 | 936 | 799 |
| Total | 16,035 | 1,124 | 17,159 | 4,479 | 12,680 |

5.6. We were informed by the CTO that they did not send NODs for District 6 in CY 2024, and that the notices were issued only in early January 2025. Further inquiry with the CTO revealed that the causes of the failure to serve said NODs were due to: (1) unknown or incomplete addresses; (2) addressee already moved out since he/she is no longer the owner of the subject property; (3) persons currently in possession of the property refused to receive the notice as they were not the addressee stated; and (5) the address has no more structure or already become a vacant lot.

5.7. A walkthrough of the processes on RPT assessment and collection revealed that the CTO generates NODs based on Statements of Account (SOA) generated through the RPTAR by the Department of Assessment (DOA). The information in the AR was based on the TDs of each RPU, such as PIN number, name and address of registered owner, market value of the land and structure, classification of the property based on its actual use, assessed and market value, and assessment level.

5.8. An interview with the DOA revealed that, based on the tax maps, the details in the AR are not updated, particularly on registered owners and addresses. The concerned personnel of DOA further averred that the last major update of the AR was in CY 2014, when the Revenue Code of Manila became effective. Since vital information in the TD is not updated, SOA and NODs have a high probability of not being effectively sent/served to intended addressees.

5.9. Furthermore, the DOA averred that the property ownership/possession frequently changes because of transactions such as transfer of ownership through sale and other forms of alienation. The DOA also stated that they were not apprised by the Register of Deeds of Manila of changes in property ownership nor furnished with the abstract of registry which includes a brief but sufficient description of the real properties entered therein, present owners, and the dates of most recent transfer or alienation accompanied by copies of corresponding deeds of sale, donation, or partition or other forms of alienation.

Submission of certified list of RPT delinquencies to the City Council and posting of NODs were not undertaken by the CTO

5.10. The CTO was unable to submit the certified list of RPT delinquencies to the City Council for assistance and enforcement purposes as required by Section 269 of RA No. 7160.

5.11. As part of due process and in compliance with Section 254 of RA No. 7160, each LGU shall post NODs in strategic locations within the City Hall and in each barangay where the subject property is located.

5.12. Inspection of the bulletin boards located in strategic locations within the City Hall revealed that no NODs were posted. Furthermore, an interview with concerned CTO personnel revealed that no NODs had been posted in the barangays where the properties were located.

5.13. Because of the foregoing, the issuance of a warrant of levy, public auction, and institution of civil action for the collection of delinquent taxes has not yet been undertaken, contrary to Section 255 of RA No. 7160.

Discrepancies between the TD vis-à-vis the actual survey of the CTO through its GIS involving 1,235 RPUs

5.14. To improve collection, the CTO implemented the GIS to monitor the current status of all RPUs of the City. The GIS enables the CTO to capture pictures of the current situation or status of RPUs, and in turn, compare the same to its TD to determine if the TD reflects the current status of said RPU.

5.15. In CY 2024, the CTO conducted a survey of 1,599 RPUs in District 1. The survey revealed that 1,235 out of 1,599 RPUs sampled have discrepancies in the TD. Discrepancies noted between TDs and their actual survey by the CTO included, among others: (1) multiple structures in one parcel; (2) structure has improvement/s; (3) no building-storey/structure declaration in the TD; and (4) actual use does not tally with the declaration.

5.16. The results of the survey were forwarded to the DOA for verification and updating purposes. Interview with concerned DOA personnel revealed that these findings are used as reference for comparison with the field assessment and appraisal sheets (FAAS), and are not conclusive. Said findings are still subject to physical verification and must be compared with the FAAS of the particular property surveyed. Furthermore, the personnel stated that if it is conclusively determined that there is a discrepancy in the TD, the DOA will conduct a reassessment for the updating of FAAS, and ultimately the updating of the TD and the AR.

5.17. Furthermore, the DOA averred that some of the discrepancies noted through the GIS were already reflected in the FAAS. However, the details in the FAAS are yet to be reflected and encoded in the TDs.

5.18. The foregoing circumstances, among others, resulted in the accumulation of tax delinquencies totaling P27.864 billion, exclusive of interest, as of December 31, 2024. This resulted in the City being deprived of vital income for the implementation of its priority PPAs for the benefit of its constituents.

observations.title: The accuracy of the Inventory account, totaling P309.908 million, as presented in the FS could not be determined due to:
observations.description:
a. Adjustments to year-end balances with net amount of P757.257 million without corresponding documentation;

b. Unreconciled differences between the OCAT records and the CGSO Reports of Physical Count of Inventories (RPCI) resulting in misclassification or misposting within Inventory sub-accounts amounting to P301.743 million;

c. Inability of the OCAT to maintain Stock Ledger Cards (SLC); and

d. Unreliability of the CGSO RPCI due to discrepancies between CGSO reports and hospitals concerned caused by: (1) incorrect cut-off; (2) non-maintenance of stock cards; and (3) inconsistencies in the preparation and submission of Summary of Supplies and Materials Issued (SSMI).

These are not in accordance with Paragraph 44 of IPSAS 12, Section 114 of the Manual of the New Government Accounting System (MNGAS) for Local Government Units (LGUs), and Section 111 of PD No. 1445.

6.1. Section 111 of PD No. 1445 states that the accounts of an agency shall be kept in such detail as is necessary to meet the agency's needs and, at the same time, be adequate to furnish the information needed by fiscal or control agencies of the government. The highest standards of honesty, objectivity and consistency shall be observed in the keeping of accounts to safeguard against inaccurate or misleading information.

6.2. Moreover, Paragraph 44 of IPSAS 12 provides that [W]hen inventories are sold, exchanged, or distributed, the carrying amount of those inventories shall be recognized as an expense in the period in which the related revenue is recognized. If there is no related revenue, the expense is recognized when the goods are distributed or the related service is rendered.

6.3. Further, Section 114 of the MNGAS for LGUs states that:

Sec 114. Perpetual Inventory Method. - Purchase of supplies and materials for stock, regardless of whether or not they are consumed within the accounting period, shall be recorded as inventory following the perpetual inventory method. Under the perpetual inventory method, an inventory control account is maintained in the General Ledger on a current basis. In addition, detailed inventory records are maintained for each inventory item.

Regular purchases shall be coursed thru the inventory account and issuances thereof shall be recorded as they take place, except those purchased out of the petty cash fund which shall be for immediate use and for stock in which case shall be charged immediately to the appropriate expense accounts.

The Chief Accountant shall maintain the perpetual inventory records comprising of Supplies Ledger Cards (SLC) for each commodity/stock, Property, Plant and Equipment Ledger Card (PPELC) for each category of plant, property and equipment and Work, Other Animals and Breeding Stocks Ledger Card (WOABSLC) for each type of livestock. Such ledger cards shall contain the details of the property, plant and equipment and livestock account in the inventory control account in the general ledger.

The General Services Officer or the Municipal Treasurer, as the case maybe, shall likewise maintain stock cards and property cards for supplies; property, plant and equipment; and work animals in their custody to account for the receipt and disposition of the same. The balance per stock card/property cards should always reconcile with the ledger cards of the accounting unit. They should also reconcile with the other property records like Acknowledgement Receipt for Equipment (ARE).

6.4. As of December 31, 2024, Inventory accounts of the City are as follows:

6.5. Analysis of the Inventory accounts disclosed the following deficiencies,

Adjustments to year-end balances without corresponding documentation

6.6. We noted that JEV No. 1002412028648 dated December 31, 2024, was drawn to reflect the adjustment to Inventory accounts based on the results of physical count of inventories for CY 2024. This is summarized as follows:

| Prior Period Adjustment | P757,256,723.12 |

6.7. It was observed that most of the inventory accounts were adjusted to reconcile book balances with the year-end inventory physical count based on the CGSO's submitted RPCI. This practice is under the Periodic Inventory Method, wherein Inventory records are updated at year-end based on the actual physical count. However, this method is contrary to the requirement of the MNGAS for LGUs, which prescribes the use of the Perpetual Inventory Method, requiring real-time tracking of inventories and records that are constantly updated.

6.8. It was also noted that the corresponding JEV is not supported by documents such as the Report of Supplies and Materials Inventory (RSMI), SSMI and Report of Issuance of Supplies (RIS), which would explain the reason for the adjustment made.

6.9. In addition, we noted that some adjustments that were charged to the Prior Period Adjustment account, such as misclassification of accounts and late recognition of transactions affecting the inventory accounts, which is not in accordance with Paragraph 44 of IPSAS 12.

6.10. Inquiry with the OCAT disclosed that monitoring and recording inventories' transactions in real-time are both tedious and time-consuming due to: (a) absence of a computerized inventory system; (b) RSMI and other required documents are not regularly received by them; and (c) inventories of the City are voluminous, low-value, fast-moving and complex.

Unreconciled differences between OCAT records and the CGSO’s RPCI resulting in misclassification or misposting within Inventory sub-accounts

6.11. A comparison of OCAT records and the CGSO's submitted RPCI revealed that the total Inventories of P301,742,922.26 are equal to the total inventories reported in the CGSO's submitted RPCI. However, evaluation of detailed inventory accounts revealed instances of misclassification within various accounts leading to discrepancies which are summarized as follows:

| Total | P301,742,922.26 | P301,742,922.26 | - |

6.12. We noted that discrepancies are caused by various errors in the classification or recording of specific accounts. Although the overall Inventory account appears to align with the RPCI, the discrepancies between various inventory accounts lead to distortion in the financial presentation of specific inventory classifications.

6.13. Incorrect classification or a lack of proper categorization may hinder the effective monitoring of inventory usage and impact the accuracy of financial reports. This may also mislead users of financial statements which may affect procurement planning and inventory management decisions.

Inability of the OCAT to maintain SLC

6.14. The absence of SLCs hinders proper tracking and reconciliation of inventory transactions, increasing the risk of misstatements, and potential inventory losses. This ongoing deficiency also impacts financial reporting accuracy and compliance with government accounting standards.

6.15. The OCAT raised concerns regarding the difficulty of maintaining SLCs due to the high volume, low-value, fast-moving, and diverse nature of the City's inventories. They are also having difficulties in enumerating all inventories due to the absence of Stock Cards from the CGSO which could be their basis. Nonetheless, the OCAT committed to start preparing and maintaining these SLCs in CY 2025.

Unreliability of the CGSO's RPCI, in view of the discrepancies between the reports of CGSO and concerned hospitals

6.16. To verify the existence and accuracy of inventories reported in the RPCI as prepared and submitted by the CGSO, selected pharmacies and property offices of the City of Manila were visited. The validation primarily focused on two significant inventory accounts: Medical, Dental and Laboratory inventory and Drugs and Medicine inventory, which reflected balances of P108,925,531.11 and P92,411,031.20, respectively.

6.17. Upon comparison of the inventory records reported in the RPCI with the actual stock records and documents maintained by the respective hospital departments and pharmacy units, several discrepancies were noted. This included inconsistencies in the recorded quantities between reports suggesting possible lapses in recording, reporting, or internal controls over inventory management.

6.18. It was also observed that various inventory items were erroneously reported twice in the RPCI, resulting in an overstatement of the total inventory balance of P20,259,647.89.

6.19. The significant discrepancies between the CGSO's RPCI and the reports of concerned hospitals were primarily caused by incorrect cut-off of transactions, non-maintenance of stock cards, and inconsistencies in the preparation and submission of SSMI.

6.20. The discrepancies between the CGSO and the hospitals records have raised concerns regarding the lack of an automated inventory system. Currently, inventory records are manually maintained and tracked using Excel sheets and cloud-based storage solutions.

6.21. The cited deficiencies affected the fair presentation of the accounts in the FS.

observations.title: The audit of the Land account disclosed the following conditions:
observations.description:
a. There are 348 land titles in the custody of the CGSO that are not registered under the name of the City, thus raising uncertainties in the ownership or rightful claim for said real properties;

b. The Land Transfer Certificate Titles (TCTs) of the City could not be traced to OCAT and CGSO records due to incomplete details in the Report on the Physical Count of Property, Plant and Equipment (RPCPPE) and SL of the Land account;

c. The AO in charge of the custody and safekeeping of the TCTs and vault is not covered with fidelity bond; and

d. The vault for TCTs is no longer suitable for safekeeping purposes due to flood damage, and wear and tear.

These conditions are contrary to Paragraph 27 of the IPSAS 1, Section 376 of RA No. 7160 or Local Government Code (LGC), and Section 4.4 of Treasury Circular No. 02-2009. Thus, the accuracy, reliability and existence of the land could not be ascertained. Further, the absence of fidelity bond of the AO and the lack of a suitable vault for TCTs exposes said documents to potential loss, misappropriation, and damage due to natural hazards.

7.1. Paragraph 27 of IPSAS 1 – Presentation of Financial Statements provides that the Financial Statements shall present fairly the financial position, financial performance, and cash flows of an entity. Fair presentation requires the faithful representation of the effects of transactions, other events, and conditions in accordance with the definitions and recognition criteria for assets, liabilities, revenue and expenses set out in IPSASs

7.2. Section 376 of the RA No. 7160 states the person in actual physical possession of government property or entrusted with its custody and control shall be responsible for its proper use and care and shall exercise due diligence in the utilization and safekeeping thereof.

7.3. Section 4.4 of Treasury Circular No. 2-2009 requires that every Officer, agent and employee, accountable for public property shall be liable for its money value in case of improper of unauthorized use of misapplication thereof, by himself or any person for whose acts he may be responsible. He shall likewise be liable for all losses, damages, deterioration due to negligence in keeping of use of property, where or not it be, at the time of such loss, damage or deterioration, in his actual custody.

7.4. The Land accounts as of December 31, 2024, are carried in the books of accounts at P4,115,067,881.59, details of which are as follows:

| Fund | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| General Fund | P3,632,565,953.18 |
| Special Education Fund | 482,501,928.41 |
| Total | P4,115,067,881.59 |

7.5. An inventory and inspection of the land TCTs of the City disclosed the following:

There are 348 land titles in the custody of the CGSO that are not registered under the name of the City, thus raising uncertainties in the ownership or rightful claim for said real properties

7.6. A review of the Inventory of Land Titles submitted by the CGSO revealed that there are 2,694 land titles under the CGSO's custody. We learned that from these, 348 land titles are not registered under the City’s name.

7.7. Upon inquiry, the CGSO stated that they are merely safekeeping the titles and have no additional information regarding them. As a result, it remains unclear whether these properties still belong to the City or have already been transferred to other owners.

7.8. Additionally, the inventory provided by the CGSO did not account for 241 land titles that were counted during the inspection. According to CGSO, the inventory list that was submitted has not been regularly updated and was prepared a few years back and turned over to the current AO.

The Land TCTs of the City could not be traced to OCAT and CGSO records due to incomplete details in the RPCPPE and SL of the Land account

7.9. A review of the SLs of OCAT and RPCPPE of the CGSO revealed that these land titles cannot be traced to the SLs and RPCPPE, which is not aligned with Paragraph 27 of IPSAS 1.

7.10. The particulars or description in the RPCPPE and SLs show either the name of the school, department, market, health center or hospital along with the cost, but does not indicate the specific land title or technical location of the properties.

7.11. Inquiry with OCAT disclosed that they only maintain a schedule of land with a generic description. The detailed descriptions of each land recorded in the books are incomplete since the majority of these lands were purchased or recorded before their assumption to office, and the previous officers did not maintain such detailed records.

The Accountable Officer in charge of the custody and safekeeping of the TCTs and vault is not covered with fidelity bond

7.12. Inquiry with the Officer-in-Charge of the Patrimonial Property under the CGSO disclosed that the staff responsible for the safekeeping of the vault and its contents is not covered with fidelity bond, contrary to Section 4.4 of Treasury Circular No. 2-2009.

The vault for TCTs is no longer suitable for safekeeping due to flood damage and wear and tear

7.13. The current vault for the Land Titles is located on the ground floor beside the Accountable Forms Section of the CTO. It was noted during inspection that the outer case already shows signs of wear and tear. Rust is visible on all sides. This current state of the vault puts a risk of further damage to the land titles inside it. Likewise, some land titles were already extremely torn, unreadable, and in terrible condition which is not in keeping with Section 376 of RA No. 7160.

7.14. As informed by CGSO, the vault was previously located in the CGSO storage room but was submerged in the flood during Typhoon Ondoy in CY 2009. Since then, it has been moved to its current location. As of audit date, the CGSO was already able to identify a location where the vault will be placed.

7.15. These conditions adversely affect the land account's accuracy, reliability and existence. Further, the non-bonding of the AO and the non-provision of a suitable vault for TCTs exposes the TCTs to potential loss, misappropriation, damage due to natural hazards.

observations.title: The following practices are not in accordance with Paragraph 66 of the IPSAS 17, and Sections 4.12 to 4.14, 5.7 to 5.8, 6 and 7 of COA Circular 2015-008 dated November 23, 2015:
observations.description:
a. No-recognition of the depreciation expense and accumulated depreciation on the Infrastructure Assets (IA) - Road Networks account with a total cost of P2.32 billion;

b. Non-preparation of the Report on Local Road Network due to the absence of data, such as the complete description and cost segregation of road components for the road projects coming from the DEPW; and

c. Non-maintenance of the subsidiary records on components of road networks.

Thus, the existence, accuracy, and validity of the balances of the IA – Road Networks account and its corresponding Depreciation Expense and Accumulated Depreciation account could not be established.

8.1. Paragraph 66 of IPSAS 17 states that the depreciable amount of an asset shall be allocated on a systematic basis over its useful life.

8.2. Sections 4.12 to 4.14 of COA Circular 2015-008, dated November 23, 2015, provide that after recognition, road networks shall be carried at their cost less any accumulated depreciation and any accumulated impairment losses. Each depreciable component of the road network shall be depreciated separately following the straight-line method of depreciation. No residual value shall be provided for the depreciable components of the road network system.

8.3. Sections 5.7 to 5.9 of COA Circular 2015-008, dated November 23, 2015, require the following:

Compute separately the depreciation for the road components taking into consideration the following factors: a) initial cost, and b) useful life. xxx

Maintain separate subsidiary ledgers for the road and its components namely a) road lot, b) road pavement, c) drainage and slope protection structures and d) other miscellaneous structures.

Provide complete description of the road and its components in the subsidiary ledger and reconcile with the Local Road Inventory and Road Map to ensure completeness.

8.4. Section 6 of the same Circular states the following:

1. The General Services Officer shall at the end of the accounting period render a Report on Local Road Network of the local government unit.

2. The total road network system shall be disclosed in the Notes to the financial statements of the Agency. (Annex B).

3. The Inventory Committee shall prepare the Report on the Physical Count of the Road Network system of the Local Government unit.

8.5. Section 7 of the Same Circular requires that:

a. Local Accountant

1. Prepare the Journal Voucher to record the beginning balance of the local road network and its components in the general ledger and the Local Road Network Ledger Card (Annex D), respectively;

2. Support the JV with the Registry of Public Infrastructures for Roads, a working paper on the distribution costs for the road components and working paper on the determination of the depreciated replacement cost for road components with no available cost per registry;

3. Keep and maintain subsidiary records for roads and road components for every road network; and

4. Prepare a lapsing schedule for the computation of depreciation of each component at the end of the year.

b. General Services Officer

1. Maintain a Local Road Inventory and Road Map;

2. Keep a complete Local Road Network Property Network Card for all roads and its components. (Annex E).

c. Provincial and Municipal Engineer

Provide the local accountant and general services officer with the complete description and cost segregation of road components for the road projects.

d. Local Chief Executive

Enjoin department heads compliance with the requirements of this Circular.

8.6. The IA - Road Networks account, as of December 31, 2024, has a book value of P2,322,914,290.14. This includes 253 items of IA with acquisition dates ranging from 2013 to 2023.

8.7. Per CGSO, the Road Networks amounting to P2,322,914,290.14 were completed in the following years:

| Year Completed | Quantity | Amount |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2024 | - | - |
| 2023 | 2 | P52,931,377.37 |
| 2022 | 2 | 37,356,156.60 |
| 2021 | 19 | 231,669,570.17 |
| 2020 and below | 228 | 2,000,957,186.00 |
| Total | 251 | P2,322,914,290.14 |

8.8. The audit of Road Networks disclosed the following:

Non-recognition of depreciation expense and accumulated depreciation on the IA - Road Networks

8.9. A review of the Lapsing Schedule and Road Networks SL of the OCAT showed that depreciation and accumulated depreciation were not recognized for the account amounting to P2,322,914,290.14 due to the absence of estimated useful life, which will be used as the basis for depreciation.

8.10. Also, there were 14 IA – Road Networks items that did not have information on their acquisition/construction dates. This affects the determination of the correct depreciation to be charged for each item.

8.11. The non-recognition of depreciation expense and accumulated depreciation is not in accordance with Paragraph 66 of IPSAS 17 and Sections 4.12 to 4.14 and 5.7 of COA Circular 2015-008.

Non-preparation of the Report on Local Road Network

8.12. An inquiry with the CGSO revealed that they have not prepared the Report of Local Road Network due to the absence of data from the DEPW, such as the Road ID/PIN, Road Name, Cost components, Description and Cost. They asserted that they only received the Consolidated Quarterly Report on Government PPA (QRPPA) from the DEPW. Such information is insufficient to fill out the details for the Report on Local Road Network. The non-preparation of the Report of Local Road Network is not in accordance with Section 6.1 of COA Circular 2015-008.

8.13. On the other hand, the Patrimonial Division of the CGSO has submitted the Report of Physical Count of IA – Road Network to the Office of the City Auditor. Per inquiry, the report was prepared based on the submitted road network infrastructure contracts and the QRPPAs that came from the DEPW and not from actual inventory taking of the Inventory Committee.

8.14. Further, the DEPW committed to exhaust all possible means to gather and collate the data required to prepare the needed reports.

Non-maintenance of subsidiary records for Road Network

8.15. A review of reports from OCAT showed that it does not maintain subsidiary records for roads and components for every road network, contrary to Sections 5.8 and 7.a.3 of COA Circular 2015-008. The road network system may be composed of road lot, road pavement, drainage and slope protection structure and other miscellaneous structures. Monitoring of additions due to construction, derecognition of cost on previous construction projects, major upgrading, concreting and drainage improvement were not undertaken by the OCAT due to the absence of subsidiary records.

8.16. Inquiry with the OCAT revealed that they were not able to prepare the subsidiary records due to insufficient data, such as the division of cost per component of the road network, the estimated useful life of depreciable components, adjustments and maintenance history.

8.17. As a result, the reliability, existence, accuracy, and validity of the balances of the IA – Road Networks account and its corresponding Depreciation Expense and Accumulated Depreciation account could not be established.

PPE items that were recorded in the RPCPPE but not in the OCAT, totaling P4.512 billion;

b. School buildings already demolished but still recorded in the OCAT records, amounting to P0.051 billion;

These conditions are not in accordance with Paragraph 27 of the IPSAS 1, Paragraph 82 of IPSAS 17, Section 147 of COA Circular 92-386, and Section 3.6 of COA Circular 2020-006. These discrepancies between the OCAT and CGSO records cast doubt on the accuracy, reliability and validity of the reported balances of Building and School Buildings. Also, the non-derecognition of demolished PPE overstated the School Buildings account by P0.051 billion.

9.1. Paragraph 27 of IPSAS 1 – Presentation of Financial Statements provides that the Financial Statements shall present fairly the financial position, financial performance, and cash flows of an entity. Fair presentation requires the faithful representation of the effects of transactions, other events, and conditions in accordance with the definitions and recognition criteria for assets, liabilities, revenue and expenses set out in IPSAS

9.2. Paragraph 82 of IPSAS 17 – Property, Plant and Equipment provides that the carrying amount of an item of property, plant and equipment shall be derecognized on disposal and when no future economic benefits or service potential is expected from its use or disposal.

9.3. Section 147 of COA Circular 92-386 dated October 20, 1992, states that the buildings and other Physical Structures shall be under the accountability and responsibility of the provincial or city general services officer, municipal mayor or punong barangay, as the case may be. He shall keep a separate and updated records of these properties and shall submit an inventory report to the provincial, city or municipal director on or before 15 day of January each year, showing, among others, the condition of the said properties.

9.4. Section 6.3 of COA Circular No. 2020-006, dated January 31, 2020, provides that the Property and accounting Units undertake collaborative procedures to ensure that all PPEs included in the RPCPPE are duly recorded in their respective records and that Property Cards (PCs) are maintained by the Property Unit, and the PPELCs maintained by the accounting unit shall be reconciled

observations.title: The six City District Hospitals could not maximize utilization of their resources due to the following PPE and Semi-Expendable items challenges that have not been addressed:
observations.description:
a. Unserviceable PPE and Semi-Expendable items amounting to P74.131 million remained undisposed;

b. Unserviceable PPE and Semi-Expendable items amounting to P45.867 million could no longer be traced in the books despite non-disposal of said items; and

c. Semi-expandable property items that are no longer used and unserviceable amounting to P1.128 million were inappropriately reported in the Waste Materials Report (WMR).

These are contrary to Part I, Section C.1 of COA-DBM Joint Circular No. 2024-1 dated January 30, 2024, or the Revised Manual on the Disposal of Government Properties, Section 4.7.10 of COA Circular No. 2022-004 dated May 30, 2022, and Section 167 of COA Circular No. 92-386, dated October 20, 1992, or the Rules and Regulations in the Supply and Property Management in the Local Governments.

11.1. Paragraph 82 of IPSAS 17 – Property, Plant and Equipment provides:

The carrying amount of an item of property, plant and equipment shall be derecognized:

(a) On Disposal;

(b) When no future economic benefits or service potential is expected from its use or disposal.

11.2. Section C.1 of Part I of COA-DBM Joint Circular No. 2024-1, dated January 30, 2024, provides:

The Property/Division/Section/Unit of government entities/ROs/FOs concerned shall submit to the Disposal Committee the following accomplished forms or equivalent document, as appropriate:

a. Inventory and Inspection Report of Unserviceable Property (IIRUP) – this report shall be used to account for all government properties of an entity that are subject to disposal and serves as the basis for derecognizing the government properties carried in the PPE accounts, which shall be accompanied by any of the following, as the case may be:

1. Individual survey report, duly certified by the Supply Officer and the supervisor of the Supply Officer;

2. List of missing spare parts, duly certified by the supply Officer and the supervisory of the Supply Officer;

3. Stencils of chassis and engine numbers of motor vehicles; and

4. Current photographs showing all sides of the properties.

b. Waste Materials Report (WMR) – covers expendable materials, supplies, and consumables, including spare parts, empty containers, and remnants from destroyed or damaged fixed assets.

c. Property Transfer Report (PTR) – used when there are transfers of properties from one Accountable Officer/Agency/Fund Cluster to another Accountable Officer/Agency/Fund Cluster.

11.3. Section 4.7.10 of Annex B COA Circular No. 2022-004, dated May 31, 2022, states:

Annex A.10 – Inventory and Inspection Report of Unserviceable Semi-Expandable Property (IIRUSP). This report shall be used to account for all unserviceable semi-expandable property of any entity which is subject to disposal. It shall be prepared by the property and/or Supply Division/Unit.

11.4. Section 167 of COA Circular No. 92-386, dated October 20, 1992, states:

Disposal Procedures. – When the supplies or property of a local government unit have become unserviceable from any cause, or are no longer needed, the officer immediate accountable therefor shall return the same to the head of the department or office who shall cancel the Memorandum Receipt. If no longer needed in the department, the head of the department or office shall return the same to the general services officer, municipal or barangay treasurer, as the case may be, with the use of Property Return Slip (LGU Form No. 12). The general services officer, municipal or barangay treasurer, as the case may be shall through the local chief executive, file an application for its disposal with the provincial, city of municipal auditor who shall conduct an inspection and determination whether the subject property is with or without value.

11.5. Section 7.1.a of COA Circular No. 2020-006, dated January 31, 2020, states:

For non-existent/missing PPEs, the Property Unit shall:

(a) Verify if the PPE items were already disposed with supporting IIRUP or transferred/donated to other government agencies with supporting Property Transfer Report; and

11.7. Also, the WMR showed items of Semi-Expendable items of P1,127,856.30, pertaining to SAH and Ospital ng Tondo amounting to P852,425.00 and P275,431.30, respectively.

11.8. Actual inspection and verification of the Audit Team of the PPE and Semi-Expandable items of the six Hospitals disclosed that:

Unserviceable items of PPE, Semi-Expandable items remain undisposed

11.9. Inquiry with the Property/Supply Officer assigned in the six District Hospitals disclosed that the CGSO has yet to accept these items for disposal due to a lack of storage space. These PPE and Semi-Expandable property items take up usable space in the district hospitals, which may have been allotted for additional storage and operations. It was also noted that only unserviceable items from the old building of ONMMC were accepted by the CGSO in CY 2023.

11.10. In an interview with the CGSO, they acknowledged the lack of storage space for returned unserviceable items. To address this, future auctions for the disposal of PPE shall be conducted on an as-is-where-is basis.

11.11. The CGSO added that disposal was put on hold due to measures adopted for the ongoing one-time cleansing of PPE accounts per COA Circular No. 2020-006, which was started in the 3rd Quarter of CY 2024. The CGSO’s efforts aimed to backtrack and review all previously unserviceable items and disposal procedures, which will allow proper reconciliation of the PPE accounts. The CGSO decided to hold the disposal of unserviceable properties for CY2024 and will resume by CY 2025.

11.12. Although Section 7.1.a of COA Circular No. 2020-006 states the Property units shall verify each disposed PPE item with supporting IIRUP or transferred/donated items to other government agencies with PTR, COA Circular No. 2020-006 does not state that the disposal procedures will be put on hold. Such practices are contrary to Section 167 of COA Circular No. 92-386.

observations.title: The reliability and accuracy of the Construction in Progress (CIP) account balance totaling P4.086 billion cannot be ascertained due to:
observations.description:
a. Non-reconciliation of the OCAT records and the CGSO RPCPPE of the CIP, with discrepancies amounting to P6.532 billion due to:

Projects appearing in the RPCPPE of CIP but were not recorded in the books, amounting to P0.106 billion;

Projects that have been completed but remain recorded under CIP and have not yet been reclassified to their corresponding asset accounts amounting to P2.097 billion;

The CIP account is credited for completed projects. However, the corresponding debit entry to initially recognize the project was not recorded, amounting to P0.241 billion; and

Double recording of transactions amounting to P0.178 billion.

b. Non-maintenance of the CIP Ledger Card (CIPLC) for each project by the OCAT.

These practices are not in accordance with Paragraph 27 of the IPSAS 1, Section 16 of Chapter 1 of the MNGAS for LGUs, Volume II, and Section 111 of PD No.1445. Thus, the fairness of the CIP account balance could not be established.

12.1. Paragraph 27 of IPSAS 1 - Presentation of Financial Statements provides that the Financial Statements shall present fairly the financial position, financial performance, and cash flows of an entity. Fair presentation requires the faithful representation of the effects of transactions, other events, and conditions in accordance with the definitions and recognition criteria for assets, liabilities, revenue and expenses set out in IPSASs.

12.2. Section 111 of PD No. 1445 states that the accounts of an agency shall be kept in such detail as is necessary to meet the agency's needs and, at the same time, be adequate to furnish the information needed by fiscal or control agencies of the government. The highest standards of honesty, objectivity and consistency shall be observed in the keeping of accounts to safeguard against inaccurate or misleading information.

12.3. Further, Section 16, Chapter 1 of the MNGAS for LGUs, Volume II, requires the maintenance of a CIPLC. It is a “subsidiary ledger card to be kept for each construction in progress, which records the amount paid per billing of the contractor in case of construction by straight contract and the amount paid for materials, labor and overhead in case of construction by administration.”

12.4. In addition, Volume I of the same Manual provides that:

During construction these infrastructures shall be recorded in the books under the account “Construction in Progress”. Upon completion, the completed asset shall be transferred to the account “Public Infrastructure”. At the end of the year, completed assets under “Public Infrastructure” shall be transferred to the respective registry.

Completed public infrastructures funded out of a loan shall, however, be retained in the books of accounts until the loan is fully paid.

12.5. As of December 31, 2024, the CIP accounts of the City reported the following balances in the FS:

| Account Names | GF | SEF | Total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CIP - Infrastructure Assets | P102,561,621.83 | - | P102,561,621.83 |
| CIP - Buildings and Other Structures | 3,983,269,354.12 | P4,674,352,673.41 | 8,657,622,027.53 |
| Total CIP | P4,085,830,975.95 | P4,674,352,673.41 | P8,760,183,649.36 |

12.6. Analysis of the CIP account disclosed the following deficiencies:

Non-reconciliation of the OCAT’s records and the CGSO’s RPCPPE of the CIP with discrepancies

12.7. A comparison of OCAT records and the CGSO’s submitted RPCPPE of the CIP account disclosed a discrepancy of P6,532,249,125.22 or 75 percent of the total CIP Account. Details are summarized as follows:

| Account Names | FS | RPCPPE | Difference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CIP - IA | P102,561,621.83 | P 102,342,015.18 | P 219,606.65 |
| CIP - Buildings and Other Structures (CIP-BOS) | 8,657,622,027.53 | 2,125,592,508.96 | 6,532,029,518.57 |
| Total CIP | P8,760,183,649.36 | P 2,227,934,524.14 | P6,532,249,125.22 |

12.8. Our audit disclosed the following errors and omissions:

There are 10 projects appearing in the RPCPPE of CIP but are not recorded in the books

12.9. We noted 10 ongoing projects amounting to P105,786,193.03 involving the construction of infrastructure assets, buildings, and other structures that appeared in the RPCPPE of CIP but were not reported in the books. The percentage of completion of these projects ranged from 10 percent to 98 percent.

12.10. Inquiry with the OCAT disclosed that they are only made aware of project/s when billings are processed by their office. Hence, if there are no billings yet, they have no other source of information from which they can use as a basis to record ongoing projects.

Reported projects in the CIP without pertinent details. Completed projects remained recorded under the CIP-IA, not reclassified to the appropriate asset accounts

12.11. A review of the subsidiary ledgers and the submitted lapsing schedule disclosed that there were six completed projects remain recorded under the CIP account and have not been reclassified to the appropriate asset accounts. These projects were already completed in CY 2024, as reported in the Report on Government PPAs (GPPAs) as of December 31, 2024.

12.12. It was noted that among the factors that contributed to the delay in reclassifying these completed projects recorded under CIP-IA and CIP-BOS accounts is OCAT’s practice to reclassify completed projects only when all claims due to the concerned contractors have been submitted, processed and paid. This practice prevents the fair presentation of the CIP and Accounts Payable (AP) account for the period, i.e., overstated the CIP account, understated its corresponding PPE account and Accounts Payable.

The CIP account is credited for completed projects. However, the corresponding debit entry to initially recognize the project was not recorded.

12.13. We noted three transactions where the CIP account totaling P241,211,816.64 was credited for completed projects to transfer the costs to the appropriate asset account. However, during the audit, no corresponding debit entries were found in the CIP account to reflect the accumulation of project costs during the construction or development phase.

Double recording of transactions

12.14. We also noted an instance in the CIP–IA account where the same transaction was recorded more than once by the OCAT. The set up payable for 15 percent advance payment for the construction of San Sebastian Residences located at Quiapo, Manila amounting to P178,199,685.71 were recorded twice under JEV Nos. 1002207014007 and 1002203004594.

12.15. The double recording resulted in the overstatement of the CIP Account.

Non-maintenance of the CIPLC for each project

12.16. The OCAT did not maintain CIPLC pursuant to Section 16, Chapter 1 of the MNGAS for LGUs, Volume II, which mandates the maintenance of subsidiary ledgers to monitor the status and balances of ongoing infrastructure projects. This hindered the proper monitoring, validation, and reconciliation of expenditures charged to the CIP account.

12.17. These deficiencies made it challenging to reconcile the OCAT records with the results of the physical count conducted by the CGSO and the reports from the implementing office/s and affected the fair presentation of the CIP, PPE, and AP account in the FS.
