observations.title: The Due to BIR account amounting to P577.243 million could not be established due to the existence of:
observations.description:
a. Unremitted/unreconciled taxes withheld, including those from prior years amounting to P491.145 million, which is not in compliance with BIR revenue regulations; and

b. Abnormal (debit) SL balances totaling P527.375 million, contrary to IPSAS.

Thus, the accuracy and fairness of the Due to BIR account cannot be ascertained.

14.1. IPSAS 1 – Presentation of Financial Statements relates accruals to the recognition of transactions and events as they occur and not when cash or its equivalent is received/paid. This means that goods or services acquired by the Organization but not yet paid for should be accrued in the period in which they were received.

14.2. Section 111 of the PD No. 1445 states that the accounts of an agency shall be kept in such details as is necessary to meet the needs of the agency and at the same time be adequate to furnish the information needed by fiscal or control agencies of the government. The highest standards of honesty, objectivity and consistency shall be observed in the keeping of accounts to safeguard against inaccurate or misleading information.

14.3. Revenue Memorandum Order No. 23-2014 dated June 20, 2014, reminded government agencies, including LGUs, of their obligations, as withholding agents, to deduct, withhold and remit taxes within the time prescribed by law. Under Revenue Regulation No. 2-98 dated April 17, 1998, government agencies were required to remit all taxes withheld on or before the 10th day of the succeeding month.

14.4. The BIR issued Revenue Memorandum Circular No. 47-2023 dated May 03, 2023, which reiterates the proper time of remittance of withholding taxes by National Government Agencies, Instrumentalities, Local Government Units, and Government-Owned and Controlled Corporations which was already required under Revenue Regulations (RR) No. 12-2001, amending section 2.57.4 of RR No. 2-98, which provides that:

Section 4. Time of Withholding - Section 2.57.4 of RR2-98, is hereby amended to read as follows:

Section 2.57.4 Time of Withholding - The obligation of the payor to deduct and withhold the tax under Section 2.57 of these Regulations arises at the time an income payment is paid or payable, or the income payment is accrued or recorded as an expense or asset, whichever is applicable, in the payor's books, whichever comes first. The term "payable" refers to the date the obligation becomes due, demandable or legally enforceable.

Provided, however, that where income is not yet paid or payable but the same has been recorded as an expense or asset, whichever is applicable, in the payor's books, the obligation to withhold shall arise in the last month of the return period in which the same is claimed as an expense or amortized for tax purposes. x x x

14.5. As of December 31, 2024, the Due to BIR account representing taxes withheld from employees, contractors, and suppliers as well as its remittance showed the following balances:

14.6. An evaluation of records disclosed the following:

Taxes withheld but not immediately remitted to the BIR, including those from prior years

14.7. It could be observed from the above table that taxes withheld from January to December 2024 amount to P974,994,925.32 plus the P472,844,465.67 unremitted taxes in CY 2023 and prior years, totaling P1,447,839,390.99. Meanwhile, total remittances in CY 2024 and January 2025 amounted to P870,596,844.35 and P86,096,774.37, respectively, leaving an unremitted or unreconciled balance of P491,145,772.27 contrary to BIR revenue regulations.

14.8. The unremitted or unreconciled balance of P491,145,772.27 is withheld or accrued in the following period:

| 2024 | P201,925,865.05 | P32,075,866.12 | P3,075,757.83 | P237,077,489.00 |

| Total | P388,035,112.31 | P72,400,744.50 | P30,709,915.46 | P491,145,772.27 |

14.9. The account includes taxes withheld in connection with year-end payables to be remitted the following year upon payment of amounts due to suppliers and contractors.

14.10. Furthermore, a portion of the unremitted or unreconciled balances, amounting to at least P48,556,602.80, pertains to employees' compensation. Given that funds for employee compensation should be readily available, the corresponding taxes withheld should be remitted promptly. Upon inquiry, the OCAT explained that they are still in the process of reconciliation and some of these balances were remitted to the BIR in February 2025.

14.11. The non-reconciliation/non-remittance could accumulate the balance of the account and become increasingly difficult to track and verify, leading to sustained accounting discrepancies. This may impact the City's ability to make well-informed financial decisions.

Abnormal (debit) SL balances

14.12. Review of the SLs of the Due to BIR account disclosed that there are 16 SLs with abnormal (debit) balances amounting to P527,374,804.97.

14.13. It was noted that this issue is a reiteration of the prior year's observation, which previously reported an abnormal (debit) balance of P395,086,747.00 that needed to be reconciled. However, the balance further increased by P132,288,057.97, bringing the total to P527,374,804.97 due to the erroneous double recording of adjusting entries.

14.14. Further, the abnormal balances reported in the SEF and TF resulted from excess of debit entries over credit entries made in CY 2024. Thus, reconciliation of these remain feasible.

14.15. The OCAT acknowledged that abnormal SL balances resulted from posting errors in accounting entries, particularly the misclassification of tax remittances and accruals to incorrect accounts.

14.16. The abnormal SL balances indicate that the City remitted more taxes than were actually withheld or due, which require a tax refund or tax credit application. This highlights the need for enhanced monitoring and accurate processing of tax withholdings and remittances, particularly for compensation and contractor payments. These underscores the need for strengthened controls and reconciliation measures.

14.17. Thus, the accuracy and fairness of the Due to BIR account balance of December 31, 2024, could not be ascertained.

15.1. Paragraph 27 of IPSAS 1 – Presentation of Financial Statements provides that the FS shall present fairly the financial position, financial performance, and cash flows of an entity. The remittance by the government agency of the contributions to the GSIS shall take priority over and above the payment of any and all obligations, except salaries and wages of its employees.

Section 15 - Interest on Delayed Remittance

The government agency shall be imposed interest for every month of delay, or a portion thereof, in the remittance of the monthly premium contributions and other amounts due the GSIS, at the rate of 2% per month simple interest. Unreconciled balances for premium contribution and for various service loans availed by the city employees, between the amounts recorded in the books and the GSIS billing statements, were due to gaps in procedures and policies

15.10. Records of the OCAT disclosed that the amount recorded for due and demandable premium contributions as of December 31, 2024, totaled P18,944,435.56, while the billing statement from the GSIS amounted to P59,665,892.08, hence, a discrepancy of P40,721,456.52

15.11. Furthermore, OCAT records showed that the amount of loan amortizations recorded in the books as of December 31, 2024, amounted to 142,471,342.12, while the billing from the GSIS totaled P192,079,519.71, showing a discrepancy totaling P49,608,177.19.

15.12. The following procedural gaps were noted during the walkthrough of procedures and inquiries made to the OCAT and the City Personnel Office (CPO), which are not aligned with Sections 14, 15 and 16 of RA No. 8291 and its RIRR and GSIS Memorandum Circular No. 027, s. 2021:

a. The payroll system of the City is not centralized; i.e. each office/department prepares its payroll through designated Department Personnel Officers (DPOs), including the determination of mandatory deductions such as GSIS contributions, HDMF contributions, PhilHealth Contributions, etc., hindering the reconciliation of records from OCAT, GSIS and CPO;

b. The basis of the OCAT in recording remittance of premium contributions and loan amortizations due to GSIS are the DVs prepared by the DPO of each department/office;

c. The DPOs are tasked with updating membership data records, addressing any mismatched data of each employee, and preparing the ARA for submission to the GSIS;

d. The AAOs of each department/office of the City are tasked with preparing the payroll for its employees. However, there is no coordination with DPOs, which causes critical information, such as salary discrepancies due to promotions and salary increments, to be excluded from the ARAs prepared by the DPOs.

e. The AAOs are also responsible for approving the loan applications of City employees. However, since the AAOs of each department/office do not report to the DPOs, CPO and the OCAT on the status of the members’ GSIS accounts, the OCAT, CPO, nor the DPOs have no individual ledgers of employees who had availed of various GSIS service loans for monitoring and consolidating reports and members’ requests for updates of critical information.

15.13. Inquiries with concerned City officials disclosed that the main reason for the unreconciled amounts pertaining to premium contributions is the presence of unmatched records between the generated Electronic Billing File (EBF), GSIS eBCS and the ERF uploaded by the City. The eBCS requires all uploaded ERFs to be 100 percent matched against the GSIS database. The mismatched records include those without Business Partner (BP) Numbers, salary discrepancies due to promotions and salary increments, inactive members, etc. Remittances with mismatched data were therefore rejected by the GSIS system, resulting in unreconciled amounts recorded in the books and actual billing of GSIS for premium contributions amounting to P5,446,445.36.

15.14. According to the concerned City officials, these mismatched data were due to the late submission of the ARA by DPOs, which is the basis for updating the membership profile to reflect the new salary rate, employment status, position and other important information. Furthermore, there are cases in which the DPOs did not promptly address the mismatched data by timely submitting the necessary membership updating forms to the GSIS.

15.15. As for the various loan services availed by the employees of the City, the OCAT averred that the unreconciled amounts were due to employees who availed various service loans but opted to pay over-the-counter (OTC). The loans of these employees were approved by the AAOs, but the employees chose not to deduct the loan amortizations due from their salaries and elected to pay over the counter. The AAOs were not able to monitor the payments made by the employees OTC since they do not maintain individual ledgers for monitoring the employees who had availed of various service loans from the GSIS. The OCAT further averred that they only remit loan amortizations directly deducted from employees’ salaries every payroll period. The OCAT stated that they have no tool to monitor the employees’ payments through OTC since the AAOs do not monitor and maintain a database of the OTC payments. These circumstances resulted in an unreconciled balance of loan amortizations recorded in the books compared to the billing statement of the GSIS amounting to P49,608,177.19.

15.16. The OCAT claimed that these unreconciled balances are “clarificatory items” and that the City is currently in constant communication with GSIS regarding reconciling these discrepancies.

15.17. Thus, the GSIS account balance cannot be accurately determined. Additionally, the gaps in procedures and policies and the discrepancies noted expose the City and its employees to unnecessary interest and affect the employees’ loan privileges and other benefits from the GSIS.

16.1. Section 3, Rule VII of the IRR of RA No. 9679 provides in part:

No. 9679 and these Rules shall be liable for their payment, and non-payment thereof shall further subject the employer to a penalty of three percent (3%) per month of the amounts payable from the date the contributions fall due until paid.

16.2. Further, Paragraph 27 of IPSAS 1 – Presentation of Financial Statements states that Financial Statements shall present fairly the financial position, financial performance and cash flows of an entity. Fair presentation requires the faithful representation of the effects of transactions, other events and conditions in accordance with the definitions and recognition criteria for assets, liabilities, revenue and expenses set out in IPSASs. observations.title: The balance of Due to PhilHealth account under the GF amounting to P43.517 million could not be ascertained due to:
observations.description:
a. Unreconciled/unremitted balance amounting to P29.998 million and delayed remittance for a period of 16 to 787 days during the year;

b. Errors in recording transactions in the SLs amounting to P7.513 million; and

c. Delay in the recording of remittances in the books totaling P25.571 million.

Thus, the accuracy and fairness of the Due to PhilHealth account cannot be ascertained. Likewise, the delayed remittances may expose the City to liability in paying the interest and penalties prescribed by PhilHealth and other penalties as provided by the IRR of the National Health Insurance Act of 2013.

17.1. IPSAS 1 states that financial statements shall present fairly the financial position, financial performance, and cash flows of an entity. Fair presentation requires the faithful representation of the effects of transactions, other events, and conditions in accordance with the definitions and recognition criteria for assets, liabilities, revenue, and expenses set out in IPSASs.

17.2. The Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting indicates that verifiability is one of the qualitative characteristics that enhances the usefulness of the information and helps assure users that the said information faithfully represents the economic phenomena it purports to represent. Verifiability necessitates that the balance in a particular account can be verified as to its existence.

17.3. Section 18(b), Rule III, Title III of the Revised IRR RA No. 7875 or the National Health Insurance Act, as amended by RA No. 9241 and RA No. 10606, provides that: The monthly premium contribution of employed members shall be remitted by the employer on or before the date prescribed by the Corporation.

17.4. Also, PhilHealth Circular No. 0001, s. 2014, on the New Payment Schedule for Premium Contributions, instruct that:

The payment schedule for the applicable month starting March 2014 onwards for the Formal Sector, specifically all Government and Private employees is hereby revised as follows:

| Existing | New Payment Schedule |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Every 10th day of the month following the applicable period | Employers with PENs ending 0-4 | Every 11th-15th day of the month following the applicable period |
|  | Employers with PENs ending 5-9 | Every 16th-20th day of the month following the applicable period |

Submission of reports shall be within five (5) days after payment. Consistent to PhilHealth Circular No. 27 s. 2010, should the date due fall on a weekend or on a holiday, payment and report submission shall be made on the next working day.

17.5. Further, section 11 of the Revised IRR of the National Health Insurance Act of 2013, prescribed that: Failure to timely remit the appropriate premium and contribution shall be subject to interest and penalties as prescribed by the Corporation without prejudice to other applicable penalties.

17.6. Section 123 of PD No. 1445, otherwise known as the Government Auditing Code of the Philippines, defines internal control: Internal control is the plan of organization and all the coordinate methods and measures adopted within an organization or agency to safeguard its assets, check the accuracy and reliability of its accounting data, and encourage adherence to prescribed managerial policies.

17.7. As of December 31, 2024, the Due to PhilHealth account, representing premium contributions of employer and employee, showed a balance of P43,517,382.69. The City maintained three SLs for the account of Due to PhilHealth. The balance of the said accounts as of December 31, 2024, are in the succeeding table.

| Due to PhilHealth | 2-02-01-040 | P7,513,357.06 |

17.8. A review of the Due to PhilHealth account of the City revealed the following observations:

Unreconciled/unremitted balance and delayed remittance during the year

17.9. An analysis of the withholding and remittance of PhilHealth contributions for employees revealed that the City withheld P168,132,068.13 and remitted P158,313,748.56 during the year leaving a balance of P43,517,382.69, as follows:

| Particulars | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Beginning Balance, Jan 1, 2024 | P33,699,063.13 |
| Add: Contribution withheld from Jan to Dec 2024 | 168,132,068.12 |
| Total Contribution for remittance to PhilHealth | 201,831,131.25 |
| Remittance to PhilHealth from Jan to Dec 2024 | 158,313,748.56 |
| Balance as of Dec 31, 2024 | 43,517,382.69 |
| Less: January 2025 Remittances/ Adjustments | 13,519,330.30 |
| Unremitted/unreconciled Balance | P29,998,052.39 |

17.10. Inquiry with the OCAT disclosed that they are still in the process of reconciling the amount of P29,998,052.39, and the same will be remitted once reconciliation is completed.

17.11. Also, the CTO stated that most of the delays in remittance were due to DVs with attached special payrolls. Accordingly, payrolls may be categorized as regular payroll and special payroll. Regular payroll pertains to the monthly payroll of the City employees, which have no adjustments as to the computation of their basic monthly pay. On the other hand, special payroll pertains to the payroll of newly hired or regular employees who have insufficient leaves, resulting in adjustments to their basic pay. Due to adjustments in the computation of salaries, including the withholding and remittance of PhilHealth premiums, the vouchers for special payroll remittance were not promptly submitted to the CTO, resulting in a delay in the remittance of the withheld premium contribution.

17.12. It was also noted that the City’s PEN is 150774000001, and as such, is required to make a premium contribution to PhilHealth every 11th to 15th day of the following month. However, the audit revealed that the City was delayed by 16 to 787 days in the remittance of PhilHealth premium contribution of their employees, contrary to PhilHealth Circular No. 0001, s. 2014.

Errors in recording transactions in the SLs

17.13. An inquiry with OCAT personnel disclosed that the first two SLs were the accounts used to classify the contribution of the premium between the share of the City and by the share of the City employees, respectively. While the last SL should have no balance; however, an amount of P7,513,357.06 was recorded in the SL. Per inquiry with OCAT, the balance may be due to various incorrect encodings in their journal and they are reconciling their records to correct them and these transactions to be posted to their appropriate SL accounts.

Delay in the recording of remittances

17.14. The process of remittance of the PhilHealth premium contribution of the City starts from the preparation and submission of payroll documents of 41 offices/departments of the City to the OCAT for proper recording and checking. Within the OCAT, the amount of the remittance will be verified by their RPT Accounts Division, which will eventually be forwarded to the CTO for the issuance of check and eventual payment to proper payees. The recording of the remittance will be entered in the books upon the return of the vouchers to the OCAT.

17.15. Analysis of the recording in the books of the PhilHealth remittances revealed that the City failed to record timely the remittances totaling P25,570,966.43. A significant portion of the delayed recording was due to the remittances for January and February of CY 2024, which were only recorded in August of the same year.

17.16. The delay in recording the remittances was due to improper control of documents, including the preparation of the payroll, transmittal of documents, and return of the same for recording. The delay in the recording affects the accuracy of financial reporting by bloating both the value of the liability account and the cash in the bank account during the period it was still unrecorded.

17.17. Thus, the accuracy and fairness of the Due to PhilHealth account cannot be ascertained. Likewise, the delayed remittances may expose the City to liability in paying the interest and penalties prescribed by PhilHealth and other penalties as provided by the IRR of the National Health Insurance Act of 2013.

observations.title: The determination of whether intended projects were implemented in compliance with Section 6.7 of COA Circular No. 94-013 and COA Circular No. 2012-001, could not be performed due to the following:
observations.description:
a. Fund transfers from various NGAs aged more than five years totaling P97.852 million remained unliquidated due to the absence of supporting documents and reports to establish whether intended projects were implemented or not; and

b. Donations received totaling P22.599 million remained outstanding for more than 5 years due to the absence of Deeds of Donation or equivalent documents to support the basis of its utilization.

These conditions adversely affect the fairness of the presentation of the Due to NGAs account in the FS, contrary to Paragraph 27 of IPSAS 1.

18.1. Paragraph 27 of IPSAS 1 – Presentation of Financial Statements provides that the FS shall present fairly the financial position, financial performance, and cash flows of an entity. Fair presentation requires the faithful representation of the effects of transactions, other events, and conditions in accordance with the definitions and recognition criteria for assets, liabilities, revenue, and expenses set out in IPSASs.

18.2. Section 6.7 of COA Circular No. 94-013 states that the IA shall return to the SA any unused balance and refund of disallowance upon completion of the project.

18.3. Likewise, Items 3.1 and 3.2 of COA Circular No. 2012-001, dated June 14, 2012, provide general guidelines on the transfer of funds to implementing agencies and from TF to GF for unspent balance/excess amount:

3.1 Transfer of funds to Implementing Agencies

Fund transfers should be properly taken up in the books of both agencies, used only for the purpose intended, and properly accounted and reported (COA Circular No. 94-013 dated December 13, 1994):

xxx

3.1.2 Implementation and Liquidation

Implementing Agency:

Necessary supporting documents depending on the nature of transactions

Copy of MOA/Trust Agreement xxx

3.2 From Trust Fund to General Fund for unspent balance/excess amount

Report of receipt, Disbursement and Fund Balance certified by Accountant

Contract, which may be a MOA, Trust Agreement or Memorandum of Understanding governing the utilization of funds and disposition of any balance thereof after completion of the purpose of the funds transferred

Letter of IA to the Source Agency to transfer the unexpected balance to the General Fund duly approved by the Source Agency, of the disposition thereof has not been provided in the MOA, Trust Agreement or Memorandum of Agreement

18.4. As of December 31, 2024, the balance in the Due to NGA account in the TF was P964,078,359.63.

18.5. A review of the SL and other audit procedures revealed the following:

Fund transfers from various NGAs aged more than five years remained unliquidated due to the absence of pertinent documents and reports as a basis for determining whether the intended projects were already implemented or not.

18.6. Scrutiny of SLs revealed that the account includes P97,851,593.39 intended for the implementation of 110 PPAs.

18.7. Inquiry with the OCAT revealed that these are long-standing outstanding balances that originated from the old accounting system and were carried over and migrated to the new accounting system in CY 2019. There have been no movements on these accounts since CY 2019. Furthermore, the OCAT averred that there are no Memorandum of Agreement (MOA), Trust Agreement (TA), Liquidation Report and Status of Utilization or other similar documents in support of said fund transfers from various NGAs to determine the status of project implementation. Hence, not in compliance with COA Circular 2016-005 and Section 6.7 of COA Circular No. 94-013.

18.8. Moreover, the balance of the Due to NGAs accounts could not be ascertained due to the absence of documents to prove that these funds were already expended/implemented or were not availed at all, which is contrary to Paragraph 27 of IPSAS 1.

18.9. The audit team emphasizes the importance of securing and retaining copies of MOA or similar documents to monitor the various fund transfers received by the City from NGAs, ensuring the proper implementation of programs. Moreover, the Liquidation and Utilization Reports will serve as monitoring tools to ensure the City’s compliance with the MOA provisions and to ensure the OCAT's proper recording of transactions.

Donations received by the City remained outstanding for more than five years due to absence of Deed of Donation or similar documents, which shall be the basis of utilizing the same.

18.10. Donations received by the City, amounting to P22,599,384.58 million, which pertained to 28 PPAs, remained unliquidated as of audit date due to lack of Deeds of Donation or other similar documents, as well as utilization reports.

18.11. Examination of the nature of some donations revealed that activities for which the donations were allocated have already been concluded, such as COVID-19 donations and donations for Typhoons Sendong and Ondoy.

18.12. The OCAT stated that these donations were not supported by Deeds of Donation or other similar documents. Further, OCAT averred that they have no information as to when these donations were received, as they do not possess any deed of donation that supports the same. This make it difficult to determine the status of project implementation or activities for which the donations were received.

observations.title: The present monitoring mechanism for managing the delayed recording of transactions in the books was not effective, thereby resulting in frequent adjustments totaling P414.963 million, contrary to Paragraph 27 of IPSAS 1 and Paragraphs 46 and 47 of IPSAS 3. This resulted in the restatement of the FS, which may adversely affect future fiscal planning.
observations.description:
19.1. Paragraph 27 of IPSAS 1 provides [F]inancial statements shall present fairly the financial position, financial performance and cash flows of an entity. Fair presentation requires the faithful representation of the effects of transactions, other events and conditions in accordance with the definitions and recognition criteria for assets, liabilities, revenue and expenses set out in IPSASs. The application of IPSASs, with additional disclosures when necessary, is presumed to result in financial statements that achieve a fair presentation.

19.2. Likewise, Paragraphs 46 and 47 state:

46. Errors can arise in respect of the recognition, measurement, presentation, or disclosure of elements of financial statements. Financial statements do not comply with IPSASs if they contain either material errors, or immaterial errors made intentionally to achieve a particular presentation of an entity’s financial position, financial performance, or cash flows. Potential current period errors discovered in that period are corrected before the financial statements are authorized for issue. However, material errors are sometimes not discovered until a subsequent period, and these prior period errors are corrected in the comparative information presented in the financial statements for that subsequent period. xxx

47. Subject to paragraph 48, an entity shall correct material prior period errors retrospectively in the first set of financial statements authorized for issue after their discovery by:

a. Restating the comparative amounts for prior period(s) presented in which the error occurred; or

b. If the error occurred before the earliest prior period presented, restating the opening balances of assets, liabilities and net assets/equity for the earliest prior period presented.

19.3. COA Circular No. 2015-009 or the Revised Chart of Accounts defines Prior Period Adjustments as transactions or adjustments affecting nominal accounts which are recorded only in the current year but relate to previous years. The balance of this account is closed to the Government Equity account at year-end.

19.4. As of December 31, 2024, the balance of the PPA account disclosed net credit balances of P342,809,281.64 and P666,824,361.46 in the GF and SEF, respectively.

19.5. A review of the SL of the PPA account revealed that the following transactions affected the account:

| Account | Amount | Remarks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Property, Plant, and Equipment | P281,937,127.51 | Late set-up of payable to two contractors due to delayed submission of the DVs and other documents to the OCAT. |
| Medical Supplies | 84,444,359.45 | Payments that were made to various suppliers for medical supplies delivered to the six district hospitals of the City in prior years. The corresponding payable and expenses were not recorded on time due to the late submission of the Acceptance and Inspection Report (AIR)/Delivery Receipts (DR) and other similar documents. |
| Inventory- Consumable | 16,786,042.24 | Pertains to payment made for the delivery of food packs to the Department of Social Welfare. The corresponding payable and expenses were not recorded on time due to the late submission of the DVs and other relevant documents, such as AIR and DR, to the OCAT. |
| Security Services | 13,348,293.72 | Payments that were made to two security agencies for the services rendered in CY 2022. |
| Office Supplies | 4,675,360.94 | Payments that were made to various suppliers for supplies delivered to various offices/departments of the City. The corresponding payable and expenses were not recorded on time due to the late submission of the DVs and other relevant documents, such as AIR and DR, to the OCAT. |
| Other Maintenance and Operating Expenses | 13,771,432.50 | Payments that were made to various suppliers for goods and services delivered to the City in prior years. |
| Total | P414,962,616.36 |  |

19.6. Inquiry with the OCAT revealed that these prior period adjustments primarily resulted from the delayed submission by the end-users of pertinent documents, including the AIR/DR, RIS/RSMI, billings/SOA, progress billings for infrastructure projects, and other similar evidence. Despite the issuance of the CBO’s instructions in the prior year to all departments to promptly submit all claims, frequent delays in document submission persisted, resulting in transactions being recorded in the incorrect period.

19.7. Addressing the delay of submission will minimize the frequent need for PPA adjustments, thus eliminating potential distortion of accounting data that may adversely affect the City’s future fiscal planning.

observations.title: The City fell short of its overall revenue projections by P6.783 billion or 36.67 percent primarily due to insufficient periodic monitoring and review of underperforming income accounts, contrary to Section 316 of RA No. 7160 or the LGC of 1991, LBC No. 152 dated August 2, 2023, and Budget Operations Manual (BOM) for LGUs 2023 Edition. This revenue shortfall hindered the City’s ability to fulfill its obligations to creditors and implement its PPAs.
observations.description:
20.1. Section 316 of RA No. 7160, or the LGC of 1991 provides the composition, duties and functions of a City’s Local Finance Committee (LFC), which includes determining the income reasonably projected as collectible for the ensuing fiscal year.

20.2. In addition, Chapter 5, Part II of the BOM for LGUs 2023 Edition requires the preparation of Quarterly Report of Receipts (Local Budget Accountability [LBAc] Form No. 1) to monitor income/revenue/borrowings and establish the variance between estimated and actual receipts.

20.3. For CY 2024 Annual Budget, the City projected to collect revenue totaling P18,497,389,047.00, net of National Tax Allotment (NTA) and non-income receipts, to finance its major PPAs. The income classifications are as follows:

| Income Classification | Projections |
| --- | --- |
| Tax Revenue - Individual and Corporation | P128,250,000.00 |
| Tax Revenue - Property | 9,480,000,000.00 |
| Tax Revenue - Goods and Services | 6,219,200,000.00 |
| Tax Revenue - Fines and Penalties | 77,964,349.00 |
| Service Income | 1,426,098,800.00 |
| Business Income | 1,165,162,662.00 |
| Miscellaneous Income | 713,236.00 |
| Total | P18,497,389,047.00 |

20.4. On the other hand, projected Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses (MOOE) amounted to P10,539,702,031.00, net of Special Purpose Appropriations and Confidential Fund.

20.5. Comparison of the Annual Budget projections vis-à-vis actual collections in the Statement of Financial Performance as of December 31, 2024, revealed that the City was not able to meet its revenue targets by P6,783,460,505.32 or 36.67 percent, which is not aligned with Section 316 of RA No. 7160, and LBC No. 152 dated August 2, 2023, or the BOM for LGUs 2023 Edition.

20.6. Eight accounts exceeded their target by P83,211,097.20; 15 accounts fell short of the projected income by P6,954,000,149.89; and 13 accounts generated P87,328,547.37 in collections without projections. As a result, the overall revenue projections were not met by P6,783,460,505.32 or 36.67 percent.

20.7. Inquiries to various departments and offices regarding the revenue collection efficiency of certain accounts revealed that the projected Real Property Tax – Basic was not achieved, despite efforts to collect delinquent taxes due to inaccurate addresses provided by the DOA. This resulted in demand letters not being received by real property owners. Also, the decrease in Business Tax collection was due to the non-renewal of several businesses. On the other hand, the targeted collection of Tax Revenue – Fines and Penalties – Property Taxes was exceeded due to the City’s strengthened efforts to impose and collect fines and penalties related to property tax collection.

20.8. For Clearance and Certification Fees, and Inspection Fees, the City claimed that the proposed City Ordinance to increase the price of permit fees from P50 to P200 was eventually vetoed. Additionally, Police Clearances were no longer collected by the City due to a PNP directive. Further, the existing City Ordinance regarding the applicable fees and rates for other fees is outdated.

20.9. As of audit date, the City is currently pursuing tax collection cases against taxpayers amounting to P9.8 billion.

20.10. It was noted that the Quarterly Report of Receipts (LBAc Form No. 1), which provides information to LFC members to identify variances and determine where the City should intensify its collection efforts, was not prepared by the CTO. Remedial actions could have been taken for income accounts that did not meet their targets if there had been proper monitoring of collections against projections.

20.11. The circumstances in which projected revenues are not realized and instances where accounts have no projections indicate a need to improve the City's forecasting system. Attaining targets provides assurance of funding for PPAs, which are also included in the Annual Budget.

20.12. The foregoing circumstances hindered the City’s ability to fulfill its obligations to creditors and effectively implement its PPAs for CY 2024.

observations.description:
22.1. Section 3 of DBM-DOF-DILG JMC No. 2020-1 dated November 4, 2020, states:

3.2.3 The LGUs shall ensure that the development projects to be funded out of the 20% DF are well-planned and procurement-and-implementation-ready.

22.2. Further, the Government Procurement Policy Board (GPPB) Circular No. 06-2019 dated July 17, 2019, provides the guidelines on the implementation of Early Procurement Activities (EPA).

observations.title: The following challenges in the implementation of the Ecological Solid Waste Management (ESWM) Act of 2000 or RA No. 9003 continue to burden the City’s effective realization of the benefits of said law, to wit:
observations.description:
a. Insufficient updating of pertinent ordinances and the SWM Plan to address the evolving conditions in the City;

b. Program goals to promote awareness through Information Education Campaign (IEC) for commercial establishments were not accomplished, and targets for growth were not adjusted to consider demographic shifts;

c. The Manila City Environment and Natural Resources Office (CENRO) has yet to be established.

The aforementioned circumstances have adversely affected the City’s enforcement of the ESWM Act of 2000.

24.1. Section 10 of RA No. 9003 outlines the role of LGUs in SWM pursuant to the relevant provisions of RA No. 7160, which makes them primarily responsible for implementing and enforcing the provisions of this Act within their respective jurisdictions.

24.2. The SWM as defined in City Ordinance No. 8371 dated November 18, 2014, refers to the purposeful, systematic control of the generation, storage, collection, transport, separation, processing, recycling, recovery, and final disposal of solid waste.

24.3. RA No. 9003, Section 16, and Resolution No. 154 mandate the SWM Board to conduct annual reviews and updates of the SWM Plan to ensure it remains effective and responsive to changing waste management needs.

24.4. Article VII of the City Ordinance No. 8371 mandates the creation of the Manila CENRO as the institutional mechanism responsible for policies, projects, and activities affecting the City’s environment and natural resources pursuant to the goals of sustainable development and climate change adaptation.

24.5. The key functions of Manila CENRO include:

a. Formulate measures for the consideration of the Sanggunian and provide technical assistance and support to the mayor in carrying out measures to ensure the delivery of the basic services and provision of adequate facilities relative to the environment and natural resources services as provided under Section 17 of RA No. 7160 or the Local Government Code particularly on Solid Waste disposal system or environmental management system and services or facilities related to general hygiene and sanitation; and

b. Develop plans and strategies and upon approval thereof by the mayor, implement the same, particularly those which have to do with environment and natural resources programs and projects xxx.

24.6. The Department of Public Services (DPS) was created through City Ordinance No. 7770 on November 17, 1992, and currently oversees SWM and environmental sanitation in Manila. Review of its functions disclosed that among its six divisions, the Operations Division is responsible for research, statistics, monitoring, enforcement, inspection, special projects, and motor pool and maintenance. Additionally, its six district offices monitor garbage collection and street sweeping operations within their respective jurisdictions.

24.7. To further enhance waste management efforts, Executive Order No. 23, s. 2022, issued on August 11, 2022, reorganized the City’s SWM Board. Under Section 4, Rule VI of the IRR, the Board is responsible for:

a. integrating barangay waste management plans into the City’s overall SWM strategy;

b. ensuring the sustainability, viability, and effectiveness of the City’s 10-year SWM Plan;

c. reviewing the SWM Plan every two years or as needed to align with local and international ecological waste management developments; and

d. coordinating the efforts of its component barangays in the implementation of the City SWM Plan.

24.8. The City enacted various Ordinances relative to ESWM, summarized as follows:

| Ordinance No. | Date | Particulars |

| 7484 | October 10, 1973 | Solid waste disposal practices, prohibition of open dumping of vacant lots, esteros, and other water courses. |
| 7510 | June 5, 1974 | Prohibiting scavenging. |
| 7695 | March 1, 1989 | Prohibiting the disposal of garbage trash, rubbish and refuse in open, uncovered or unsealed container. |
| 7849 | March 21, 1994 | Amending Section 4 of Ord. no. 7695 referring to disposal of garbage, by providing a higher penalty for violation thereof and providing sub-sections thereto. |
| 7853 | June 10, 1994 | Requiring the provision of garbage receptacles in all public utility vehicles in the City, providing for penalties for violation thereof. |
| 7866 | September 22, 1994 | Penalizing the disposal of garbage, debris and other waste materials in rivers, creeks, canals and waterways; providing penalties for violation thereof; allocating to the barangays 20% of the fine collected there from and other purposes. |
| 7876 | December 14, 1994 | Requiring all residents of, and business within, the city of manila to provide their homes and establishments with containers with which to segregate biodegradable and non-biodegradable garbage for composting and recycling, for the purpose of achieving and complying with the objectives and methods of the "zero-waste technology” and providing penalties for violation thereof. |
| 7924 | June 11, 1997 | Prohibiting dumping and discharging of garbage, refuse, sewer waste, debris, toxic waste and other pollutants from vessels, factories, commercial and industrial establishments, residential houses and other structures into manila bay. |
| 7981 | March 8, 2000 | Prohibiting unloading and stockpiling of loose gravel and sand, and other construction materials. |
| 8194 | August 18, 2009 | Amending Section 3 of Ord. No. 7404 - updating the penalties. |
| 8282 | September 3, 2012 | Banning the use of any form of plastic bags on dry goods and regulating its utilization on wet goods, as well as the use of polystyrene and similar materials as containers for "food, goods and other products" and providing penalties for violation thereof and for other purposes. |
| 8371 | November 18, 2014 | Providing environmental code for the City of Manila and establishment of Manila Environment and Natural Resources Office (CENRO). |
| 8752 | October 18, 2019 | Strict requirement for maintaining cleanliness and orderliness. |

24.9. In accordance with the mandates of RA No. 9003, the City developed its 10-year SWM Plan approved by the National Solid Waste Management Commission under Resolution No. 154, s. 2015, dated September 29, 2015. The 10-year SWM Plan set a target of 20 percent coverage for IEC activities across 896 barangays, 71 primary schools, 32 high schools, 6 city hospitals, and 70,015 commercial establishments in 2015. However, the plan does not specify whether this target applies to the entire 10-year period, a single year (2015), or on an annual basis.

24.10. The compliance audit of the City's implementation of RA No. 9003 and assessment of the proper collection and disposal system identified the following deficiencies:

Insufficient updating of pertinent ordinances and the SWM Plan to address the evolving conditions in the City

24.11. The City’s SWM policies have not effectively addressed current environmental challenges due to the insufficiency of regular updates to its 2015 to 2024 SWM Plan.

24.12. A review of the list of ordinances in the past decade revealed that only two were enacted: Ordinance No. 8371 (November 18, 2014), which established the Environmental Code and mandated the creation of Manila CENRO (yet to be implemented), and Ordinance No. 8752 (October 18, 2019), which reinforced cleanliness and orderliness requirements (Tapat Ko, Linis Ko). All other ordinances were crafted from 12 to 51 years ago.

24.13. Existing ordinances on waste management and cleanliness are mostly outdated and require strict enforcement. Fines for violations are generally minimal which encourage violators to disregard the same. Moreover, there are no well-defined procedures for collecting penalties and enforcement mechanisms.

24.14. Furthermore, although the City’s SWM Plan was approved by the National Solid Waste Management Commission under Resolution No. 154, s. 2015, (September 29, 2015), it has not been reviewed and updated annually, contrary to the requirements of RA No. 9003, Section 16, and Resolution No. 154.

24.15. The DPS averred that the SWM Plan was updated only once in CY 2022, two years prior to its expiration, with amendments made to the Waste Analysis and Characterization Study. The study focused on determining the quality and quantity of solid waste generated in the City and its disposal. It established that most of the generated waste is biodegradable, with food waste accounting for the largest portion. Additionally, plastic bags, despite their lightweight nature, account for a significant portion of the plastic waste composition in both generated and disposed waste.

Program goals to promote awareness through IEC for commercial establishments were not accomplished, and targets for growth were not adjusted to consider demographic shifts

24.16. The City's IEC campaigns fell short of the mandated 20 percent engagement target for commercial establishments, resulting in limited public awareness and non-compliance with SWM. While DPS met targets in other sectors, it did not account for demographic growth or adjust targets in the 10-year plan, despite Ordinance No. 8371, Article V, Section 10, which requires a large-scale SWM awareness campaign.

24.17. As of CY 2024, the DPS reported achieving the 20 percent target across various sectors, with totals of 3,521 for residential and 79 for schools and institutions. However, only 1,362 out of the 70,015 commercial establishments required for CY 2015 were targeted. The DPS acknowledged that the large number of commercial establishments posed a challenge and considered that a strategy will be developed to address this issue in the City’s next 10-year plan.

24.18. A review of the CY 2024 data showed that the City achieved 1,251 in the barangay household sector; however, no IEC activities were conducted in the other three target sectors. The DPS clarified that the 20 percent target applies to the overall 10-year plan and does not account for demographic changes, such as additional households, new students, or new establishments within its jurisdiction that require environmental awareness, despite the need for a massive public awareness campaign. Additionally, while the City met its targets in the three sectors, it did not consider raising these targets to reflect demographic shifts within the 10-year timeframe.

The Manila CENRO has yet to be established

24.19. It was also noted that despite the ongoing SWM initiatives of the DPS and the SWM Board, the required Manila CENRO has not been established.

24.20. Inquiry with DPS revealed that the ordinance creating Manila CENRO – defining its functions, staffing structure, funding provisions, and repealing the DPS remains pending with the City Council. It was disclosed that the delay was attributed to the change in the chairman of the Committee on Environmental Protection and Ecological Preservation, thus, the proposed ordinance is yet to be passed.

24.21. Additionally, it was noted that the City, through the DPS, utilized its own resources, including trucks and manpower, to collect waste that the residents were not able to bring out on time for the scheduled pick-up by the City’s contracted service provider.

24.22. This practice emphasizes a recurring issue of non-compliance among constituents with scheduled garbage collection, which has placed a persistent burden on City resources. It also deviates from the intent of RA No. 9003 and the City Ordinance No. 8371, both of which advocate for shared responsibility, timely waste disposal, and the efficient use of public resources.

24.23. Thus, the outdated ordinances and insufficient SWM Plan updates hindered waste management efforts. Furthermore, the limited IEC engagement and lack of target adjustments have reduced public awareness and compliance. Finally, the non-operation of Manila CENRO has hindered effective waste management enforcement, leading to uncoordinated implementation and over-reliance on limited city resources. This absence has further restricted the City's ability to fully enforce SWM policies and ensure resident accountability, contrary to Section 12 of City Ordinance No. 8371.

observations.title: The 5% share of the DPWH in the Building Permit Fees amounting to P23.797 million remained unremitted, as of December 31, 2024, contrary to Section 2 of the DPWH–DILG JMC No. 001, s. 2013. Further, the 15% share of the Office of the Building Official (OBO) amounting to P71.399 million remained unutilized contrary to Section 2 of the said JMC, thereby missing out on improvement opportunities of OBO operations had its share from Building Permit Fees been utilized.
observations.description:
25.1. Section 2 of the DPWH-DILG JMC No. 01, s. 2013, prescribed the procedural guidelines for the disposition of the 20% share as follows:

Xxx

a. Subject to existing budgetary, accounting, and auditing rules and regulations, the OBO shall automatically retain 15% of the income derived from building permits fees and other charges;

b. The Local Treasurer shall remit and credit the Five Percent (5%) of the income to the account of the DPWH Secretary under Special Account No. 154 thru the Bureau of Treasury. xxx

2.6 The concerned Building Official shall prepare a Program of Work detailing the manner how he would utilize the 15% share of his Office to be approved by the Local Chief Executive.

25.2. Finally, Section 3.0 of the same JMC provided for the authorized items of expenses covered for the 15% OBO Share as follows:

The 15% OBO fund shall cover all the necessary operating expenses of the OBO, including purchase of equipment, supplies and materials, travelling expenses, obligation expenses and sheriff’s fee and payment of prior years’ obligations not adequately funded, subject to existing budgetary and auditing rules and regulations.

25.3. The City collects fees in accordance with the requirements under the IRR of the National Building Code of the Philippines. These collections were divided into 80 percent for the City and 20 percent for the National Government. The 20 percent share of the National Government is then distributed as 15 percent to the account of the OBO for their operating and incidental expenses, and the other five percent shall be remitted to the account of the DPWH through the Bureau of Treasury.

25.4. As of December 31, 2024, the accounts pertaining to the 20 percent TF have cumulative balances amounting to P95,195,429.77, as follows:

| Account Code | Account Title | Balance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2-02-01-050-DPWH-5% | Due to NGAs - 5% Share from Building Permits Fees – DPWH | P23,796,557.81 |
| 2-99-99-990-OBO | Other Payables - 15% Share from Bldg. Permit Fees - Office of the Building Official | 71,398,871.96 |
| Total |  | P95,195,429.77 |

25.5. A review of the SLs of the TF accounts revealed that the 5 percent share of the DPWH was not remitted, and the 15 percent OBO share was not utilized, as follows:

The five percent share of the DPWH in the Building Permit Fees remained unremitted

25.6. A review of SLs of the five percent DPWH shares disclosed that the account's beginning balance amounted to P22,778,994.59. For CY 2024, the City was able to collect P1,017,563.22. Thus, the cumulative balance of the unremitted Building Permit Fees totaled P23,796,557.81 as of December 31, 2024, contrary to Section 2 of the DPWH – DILG JMC No. 001.

25.7. Inquiry with the OCAT and the CTO disclosed that they are still verifying and reconciling the amounts reflected in the books. The CTO also stated that they should immediately comply with the remittance of the five percent DPWH share, based on the approved DV, which has been duly validated for accuracy by the OCAT. They have already endorsed the OCAT with the summary of the subject collection for reconciliation and proper disposition.

The 15 percent share of the OBO remained unutilized

25.8. As of January 1, 2024, the 15 percent share had a balance of P68,336,983.77. For CY 2024, the collection pertaining to the OBO share totaled P3,061,888.19. Thus, the cumulative balances amounted to P71,398,871.96 as of December 31, 2024. This amount was not utilized for the purposes for which it was intended, which is inconsistent with Section 3 of the above JMC.

25.9. Interview with the OBO revealed that there was no Program of Work detailing how to utilize the 15 percent share was prepared for approval by the Local Chief Executive.

observations.title: The City’s implementation of the Local Climate Change Action Plan (LCCAP) cannot be ascertained due to the following conditions:
observations.description:
a. The PPAs under the LCCAP were not properly specified and appropriated in the City’s Investment Plan for CY 2024;

b. An LCCAP Core Team responsible for implementing, regularly monitoring and updating the LCCAP was not established;

c. The LCCAP was not regularly updated to address emerging/changing social, economic and environmental conditions and issues; and

d. An Annual Progress Report was not submitted to the Climate Change Commission.

These circumstances are contrary to RA No. 9729, otherwise known as the Climate Change Act of 2009 and DILG MC No. 2014-135 dated October 21, 2014, thereby resulting into lapses in monitoring of implementation of PPAs under the approved LCCAP.

26.1. ﻿﻿﻿ RA No. 9729 provides the following:

SECTION 14. Local Climate Change Action Plan. — The LGUs shall be the frontline agencies in the formulation, planning and implementation of climate change action plans in their respective areas, consistent with the provisions of the Local Government Code, the Framework, and the National Climate Change Action Plan. xxx

The LGU is hereby expressly authorized to appropriate and use the amount from its Internal Revenue Allotment (now National Tax Allocation or NTA) necessary to implement said local plan effectively, any provision in the Local Government Code to the contrary notwithstanding.

SECTION 18. Funding Allocation for Climate Change. —All relevant government agencies and LGUs shall allocate from their annual appropriations adequate funds for the formulation, development and implementation, including training, capacity building and direct intervention, of their respective climate change programs and plans.

SECTION 20. Annual Report. —LGUs shall submit annual progress reports on the implementation of their respective local action plan to the Commission within the first quarter of the following year.

26.2. Furthermore, Paragraph 3.1.1 of the DILG MC No. 2014-135 provides that the Local Chief Executive shall organize an LCCAP Core Team, that will lead, oversee and ensure that an LCCAP will be drafted, eventually approved, implemented, regularly monitored and updated when necessary.

26.3. ﻿﻿﻿Records disclosed that the City, through Resolution No. 214, s. 2021, adopted the approval of the City's initial LCCAP for CYs 2022 to 2032 on October 4, 2021. The plan was prepared and submitted by the Manila Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (MDRRMO). The Philippine Climate Change Commission, in a Letter dated May 4, 2022, confirmed receiving a copy of the plan, in compliance with DILG MC No. 2021-068, issued on June 28, 2021.

26.4. The LCCAP highlights its focus on two key areas: Climate Change Mitigation and Climate Change Adaptation. It also sets forth specific PPAs for the next 10 years, ensuring a structured approach to addressing climate-related challenges.

26.5. The LCCAP propositions that these activities be completed within a short or medium timeframe. Scorecards were assigned to each activity and classified as follows: Urgent PPAs (80 to 100% score) should be completed within three years, Necessary PPAs (60 to 79% score) should be implemented within six years, and Preferred PPAs (below 59% score) are the least priority.

26.6. The following conditions were noted during the review of relevant documents pertaining to the LCCAP:

The PPAs under the LCCAP were not properly specified and appropriated in the City’s Investment Plan during the year

26.7. Verification of the City's CY 2024 Local Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Investment Plan, prepared by the MDRRMO, revealed that it did not include a specific list of proposed climate change PPAs for implementation. A joint interview with CPDO and MDRRMO further indicated that while climate change-related projects are being implemented by various offices, identifying specific LCCAP-related initiatives in their Investment Plans remains a challenge.

26.8. An inquiry disclosed that continued lack of awareness among implementing departments resulted to non-tagging of PPAs despite this concern being raised in last year’s audit observations. Climate-related allocations are spread across various city offices, including the MDRRMO, Engineering Office, and Department of Public Services (Acting CENRO).

An LCCAP Core Team was not established

26.9. It was also observed that a LCCAP Core Team dedicated to overseeing the implementation and tracking of the PPAs indicated in the LCCAP was not created. Currently, only the MDRRMO serves as the Executive Secretary and handles LCCAP-related matters, while an Executive Order to formally designate the CPDO as the focal point is still pending. This requirement also remains incomplete under Section 7.0 of the approved LCCAP and is not compliant with Paragraph 3.1.1 of the DILG MC No. 2014-135.

The LCCAP was not regularly updated to address emerging/changing social, economic and environmental conditions and issues

26.10. Since the adoption of the LCCAP in CY 2022, the City has no notable updates, raising concerns about its effectiveness in addressing evolving social, economic, and environmental challenges. Without regular revisions, the LCCAP may not reflect changes in rapid urbanization, technological advancements, and emerging issues such as extreme weather events, economic shifts, and sustainability policies.

An Annual Progress Report was not submitted to the Climate Change Commission.

26.11. Annual progress reports have not been submitted to the Climate Change Commission, making it difficult to validate the status of climate change-related projects. Moreover, due to this lapse, the national agency responsible for assessing the City's alignment with evolving environmental challenges and policies may not be able to compile complete data on a national level.

26.12. The focal person claimed that monitoring of climate-change related PPAs is conducted through Annual Accomplishment Reports and Individual After-Activity Reports. However, these reports cover all DRRMO projects rather than being specific to LCCAP, hence, the absence of a centralized monitoring system. There are urgent PPAs listed in the LCCAP that should have been implemented within three years. However, three years (CYs 2022 to 2024) have already lapsed, but their actual implementation cannot be validated.

26.13. Without proper tagging of PPAs related to climate change projects, attainment of LCCAP goals, determining their total allocation, assessing its optimal utilization, and verifying whether it is financed under the NTA, as required, remains a challenge for both the city and in audit. The absence of LCCAP Core Team further complicates oversight and leads to more potential compliance issues.

observations.title: We reviewed the implementation of Gender and Development (GAD) PPAs for CY 2024 and observed the following:
observations.description:
a. There are 23 PPAs amounting to P27.221 million that were not implemented and 12 PPAs that were partially implemented with unutilized balance of P1.033 million, contrary to Philippine Commission on Women – Department of the Interior and Local Government – Department of Budget and Management – National Economic and Development Authority (PCW-DILG-DBM-NEDA) JMC No. 2013-01.

b. The Harmonized Gender and Development Guidelines (HGDG) tool in allocating a portion or the entirety of the budget for major programs aimed at enhancing the gender responsiveness of the City’s programs and budgets was not used as required by Section 6.4 of PCW-NEDA-DBM Joint Circular No. 2012-01.

c. The provisions of PCW-NEDA-DBM Joint Circular No. 2012-01 on the categorization of gender issues as client or organization-based were not complied with thereby making it difficult to summarize the PPAs by program.

d. The Annual GAD Plan and Budget was not submitted to the Office of the City Auditor within the period prescribed by COA Circular No. 2014-001 dated March 18, 2014.

Thus, addressing women's empowerment and gender equality issues could not be fully achieved due to the partial compliance with the above-mentioned JMC.

27.1. The PCW-NEDA-DBM Joint Circular No. 2012-01 was issued to provide the Guidelines for the Preparation of Annual GAD Budget and Accomplishment Report to implement the section on programs/projects related to GAD of the General Appropriations Act.

27.2. Section 6.4 of the same Joint Circular states:

6.4. Attributing agency major programs to the GAD budget. Attribution to the GAD budget of a portion or the whole of the budget of an agency’s major programs is a means toward gradually increasing the gender responsiveness of government programs and budgets.

6.4.1 If an agency intends to attribute a portion or the whole budget of major programs during the GAD planning and budgeting phase, it may subject the program to gender analysis using the HGDG tool. If the agency is not yet trained on the use of the tool, it may include said training in its GPB and may seek the assistance of an expert on gender analysis using the HGDG.

27.3. Moreover, PCW-DILG-DBM-NEDA JMC No. 2013-01, dated July 18, 2013, as amended by PCW-DILG-DBM-NEDA JMC No. 2016-01, prescribed the policies and procedures in mainstreaming gender perspectives in local planning, programming and budgeting; local legislation; project development, implementation, monitoring and evaluation pursuant to RA No. 9710 or “The Magna Carta of Women (MCW),” as follows:

2.3 Promote the general welfare, provide basic services and facilities and implement programs, projects and activities (PPAs) as provided for by Sections 16 and 17 of the LGC, the Philippine Plan for Gender-Responsive Development (PPGD) [1995 – 2025], the Philippine Development Plan (PDP) and other succeeding term plans;

4.1.A.5. xxx

b) GAD GFPS Executive Committee shall:

xx

iv. Ensure the effective and efficient implementation of the GAD PPAs and the judicious utilization of the GAD budget.

27.4. Lastly, Part V of COA Circular No. 2014-001 dated March 18, 2014, provides:

The Audited agency shall submit a copy of the Annual GAD Plan and Budget (GPB) to the COA Audit Team assigned to the agency within five (5) working days front the receipt of the approved plan from the PCW or their mother or central offices. as the case maybe. Likewise, a copy of the corresponding Accomplishment Report shall be furnished the said Audit Team within five (5) working days from the end of January of the preceding year.

27.5. A review of the City's Annual Budget for the CY 2024 showed that an allocation of P2,325,123,040, equivalent to 10.47 percent of the City's overall budget appropriations of P22,200,000,000.00, has been earmarked for the 172 GAD related PPAs. Details as follows:

27.6. During the year, there were 137 PPAs amounting to P2,296,649.423.00 that were implemented, 23 PPAs totaling P27,221,617.00 that were not implemented and 12 PPAs totaling P1,252,000.00 that were partially implemented.

27.7. Our audit disclosed that:

There are 23 PPAs that were not implemented and 12 PPAs that were partially implemented.

27.8. The City implemented 137 GAD PPAs with a total amount of P2,296,649,423, out of the total appropriation of P2,325,123,040.00, to address various GAD concerns and promote women empowerment in the City.

27.9. Out of the 137 implemented PPAs, 20 were found to have significant unutilized fund balances amounting to P6,231,977.05 and were carried out at no cost to the City.

27.10. We also noted that 23 PPAs, totaling P27,221,617.00, were not implemented during the year. Upon inquiry, management explained that these programs were not carried out due to scheduling conflicts. The construction of the Crisis Intervention Center for Women and Children, with an approved budget of P8,000,000.00, was not implemented because it was planned for integration into the City’s Kalinga Center. Also, the SK Mandatory Trainings, with an approved budget of P7,437,500.00, did not push through as the SK TF was insufficient to cover the costs of GAD trainings and seminars.

27.11. Furthermore, a total allocation of P1,252,000.00 for 12 GAD PPAs was not fully utilized leaving an unspent balance of P1,033,129.21. This is inconsistent with Item 2.3 of the JMC. Management clarified that the underutilization was due to changes in participants resulting in scheduling conflicts and a low number of clients seeking legal advice on gender-based violence, which prevented the City from meeting the target numbers.

Management did not use the HGDG tool to allocate part or all of the budget for major programs designed to improve the gender responsiveness of the City’s programs and budgets.

27.12. A review of the GAD Accomplishment Report disclosed that the City had no attributable programs using the HGDG. Thus, the integration of gender considerations into the agency's programs and budget which is required under Philippine law was not complied with. Even if a program is not fully dedicated to GAD, a portion of its budget should be allocated to gender-responsive initiatives utilizing the HGDG tool.

27.13. Inquiry with the Focal Person disclosed that they are yet to attend a series of trainings and seminars to capacitate them on the process of preparing the HGDG. During the year, they have already attended a briefer seminar on the said topic.

The gender issues were not categorized as client and organization-focused.

27.14. We noted in the GAD Accomplishment Report that gender issues were not categorized into client-focused and organizational-focused which is not in conformity with the provisions of PCW-NEDA-DBM Joint Circular No. 2012-01.

27.15. The Accomplishment Report only presented gender issues without categorizing them into client-focused and organizational-focused issues. The report did not clearly demonstrate how gender issues impact different areas of the organization. This oversight hinders effective tracking, evaluation, and the development of targeted strategies for addressing gender concerns. Without this classification, it becomes difficult to assess whether the programs effectively address gender concerns.

The City did not submit the Annual GAD Plan and Budget to the COA Resident Auditor within the required period.

27.16. Records show that the required GAD Accomplishment Report and Annual GAD Plan were not submitted to the COA Auditor within the required period as outlined in COA Circular No. 2014-001, resulting in delay in its timely evaluation.

27.17. The GAD Plan and Budget and GAD Accomplishment Report were submitted on February 10, 2025 and February 12, 2025, respectively, after a follow-up letter was sent by this Office.

27.18. Thus, addressing women's empowerment and gender equality issues were adversely affected and not fully achieved.

observations.title: We reviewed the operations of the Out Patient Department (OPD) of the six District Hospitals of the City for CY 2024 and observed that:
observations.description:
a. There were avoidable delays in the retrieval and release of patients’ medical records, which serve as the basis for the accurate and timely treatment of outpatient clients, to doctor’s clinics at the OPD of hospitals; and

b. Vulnerable conditions exist in the OPD that pose risks to patients’ safety and delay in the delivery of services.

c. These are contrary to the provisions outlined in the Hospital Health Information Management Manual, 4th Edition, and the Guidelines for the Planning and Design of a Hospital and Other Health Facilities issued by the Department of Health (DOH). Thus, the goal of providing efficient and effective healthcare services to outpatient clients is not attained, and also poses a risk to both patients and OPD staff.

28.1. The Hospital Health Information Management Manual 4th Edition, formerly the Hospital Medical Records Management Manual of the DOH, provides the general functions of the Health Information Management Department (HIMD) or the Department of Medical Records:

The general function of the HIMD is to provide an organized system of measuring quality patient care and to ensure that sufficient data is written in sequence of events to justify the diagnosis, warrant the treatment and end results. The department is tasked to process, analyze, maintain and safe keep all health records created/maintained in the healthcare facility in the course of healthcare facility and its supervisor are mandated to implement facility wide coordination and linkage. The department plays a key role in the generation of healthcare statistics to evidence-based medical care and management practices.

28.2. The same manual states the specific objectives and main functions of HMID that they need to accomplish in providing effective and efficient service to clients of the healthcare facility, which includes:

A. Objectives:

Improve the accessibility of the health records

Ensure the creation and maintenance of quality health records

Encourage greater utilization of healthcare facility statistics

B. Functions:

Maintain all health records in accordance with the principles and practices of efficient and effective health record management.

Maintain a comprehensive and up-to-date unit health record for each patient, ensure that all relevant information is collected and written in the record and filed correctly

Provide health records, upon request for patients’ visit to the OPD and Emergency Department (ED), and admission to the inpatient’s ward.

Ensure that all diagnostic reports/results are promptly and accurately filed in their respective patient’s record.

28.3. Furthermore, Chapter 3, Health Record Standards and Policies on Health Record Completion, provides that the patient’s health record shall be forwarded to the HIMD within 24 hours after discharge. (Emphasis supplied)

28.4. Guidelines in the Planning and Design of a Hospital and Other Health Facilities stipulate that hospitals and other health facilities must be planned and designed to adhere to appropriate architectural practices, meet prescribed functional programs, and comply with applicable codes as part of regular professional practice.

28.5. The same manual also states the following Sections:

Section 1 A hospital and other health Facilities shall be so located that it is readily accessible to the community and reasonably free from undue noise, smoke, dust foul odor, flood, and shall not be located adjacent to railroads, freight yards, children’s playgrounds, airports, industrial plants, disposal plants.

Section 3 Safety: A hospital and other health facilities shall provide and maintain a safe environment for patients, personnel and public. The building shall be of such construction so that no hazard to the life and safety of patients, personnel and public exist. It shall be capable of withstanding weight and elements to which they may be subjected.

Section 5 Patient Movement: Spaces shall be wide enough for free movement of patients, whether they are on beds, stretchers, or wheelchairs. Circulation routes for transferring patients from one are to another shall be available and free at all times.

Section 16 Fire Protection: There shall be measures for detecting fire such as fire alarms in walls, peepholes in doors or smoke detectors in ceilings. There shall be devices for quenching fire such as fire extinguishers or fire hoses that are easily visible and accessible in strategic areas.

28.6. Each district hospital is equipped with its own OPD that provides primary and comprehensive healthcare to an average of 100 to 300 patients daily. The OPD has a significant impact on hospital operations as it enables daily service to patients within the City and to some hospitals, even for non-Manila residents.

28.7. Each hospital has a Medical Records Department (MRD) located near or inside the OPD to promote the efficient release and return of patient charts, making its role necessary in the delivery of patient care.

28.8. An actual walkthrough, observation, and verification of the operations of the OPD of each of the six hospitals disclosed the following:

Avoidable delays in retrieving and releasing patients' medical records from the MRD to the respective doctor’s clinic

28.9. Patient health records are essential for medical personnel to make accurate diagnoses, prescribe appropriate medication, and develop effective treatment plans. Observations showed that patients were not called for consultation or treatment until after their medical records were retrieved and released to the respective clinics they intended to visit. Since it will take some time for the retrieval of patients records, this contributes to frequent crowding, slow queuing, and prolonged waiting times for patients to receive care.

28.10. It was also noted that the ONMMC has already adopted and utilized the E-konsulta program from the DOH. The E-konsulta is a digital electronic medical records platform that is aimed at solving the delay of medical records retrieval. Also, implementing the E-konsulta program will aid the revenue generation with PhilHealth. Further, to decongest the volume of patients in the ONMMC and maximize the time of their patient, they are conducting information dissemination on health issues to patients during their waiting time and capacitating the health centers.

28.11. Further observation of the processes of the MRD for the retrieval and release of outpatients' medical records revealed the following:

Delayed Delivery of services in the GABMC. The patient shall be assigned a separate scheduled consultation date, not on the same day they visited the OPD triage for assessment. However, should the patient require admission or be referred to an emergency service, as determined in the triage area, the OPD triage nurse shall assist immediately the patient and properly endorse the patient to the emergency room.

The MRD of ONT maintains electronic records using Microsoft Excel, which is not a database management program and may put patient data at risk of corruption. Microsoft Excel is a spreadsheet program, and does not have the ability to establish relationships between different tables or datasets. It also heavily relies on manual processes, making it prone to errors. Additionally, Microsoft Excel is vulnerable to unauthorized access and file corruption.

Hazards present in the OPD put OPD Staff and patients at risk

28.12. Ocular inspection of the OPD of the hospitals showed the following conditions that affects patient safety during the waiting and hinder the delivery of efficient and effective medical services to the outpatients such as waiting areas of the ONS, JJASGH and SAH in Open-Air Spaces; numerous oxygen tanks are stored along the corridor of the ONT Triage Area; and absence of Fire Protection in the OPD of ONS.

28.13. These circumstances are not in accordance with Sections 1, 3, 5, and 16 of the DOH Guidelines in the Planning and Design of a Hospital and Other Health Facilities, thus adversely affecting the attainment of the hospitals’ goal of providing efficient and effective healthcare services to its outpatient clients.

recommendations.text: Require the OIC - Medical Records Department, in coordination with the OIC - Information Technology, to formulate a program that will establish a database of electronic/scanned copies of patient records or adopt the E-konsulta system of the DOH for speedy retrieval and availability of patient files to concerned medical departments; and a queuing system that will cater to the OPD;
